entries.title: Andhra Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Andhra cuisine: the Guntur chilli and India's hottest food, gongura and the sour palate, rice with pappu and podi, and the split between coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema and Telangana.
entries.text: andhra cuisine andhra cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of andhra cuisine: the guntur chilli and india's hottest food, gongura and the sour palate, rice with pappu and podi, and the split between coastal andhra, rayalaseema and telangana. andhra cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana south india andhra cuisine the hottest and the sourest kitchen in india, built on chilli from guntur, tamarind, gongura leaf and a mountain of rice. the guntur chilli, and why andhra burns chilli reached india with portuguese traders in the sixteenth century and landed on a coast that was ready for it. the black soils around guntur, in the krishna delta, turned out to suit the crop better than almost anywhere else, and the district became the centre of an industry: andhra pradesh now grows the largest share of india's chilli, the guntur market yard is among the biggest in asia, and the guntur sannam variety carries a geographical indication tag. what began as an import became the single ingredient the cuisine is identified by. the heat is not decorative. chilli goes in whole and dried into the tempering, ground wet into pastes for curries, and dry-roasted into powders eaten straight with rice, so a single meal delivers it three different ways. a rayalaseema kodi kura can carry more chilli by weight than any other indian home dish, and the region's cooks distinguish carefully between varieties chosen for colour, such as the deep-red byadgi grown to the west, and those chosen for pungency. outsiders read this as machismo. locally it is closer to seasoning logic: in a hot, dry climate with limited refrigeration, chilli preserved food, drove appetite and made a plain plate of rice worth eating. gongura, tamarind and a taste for sour if chilli is the loud half of the palate, sourness is the half that actually organises the meal. gongura, the leaf of the roselle plant, is the emblem: coarse, oxalic-sharp, thriving on dry land that will not support much else. cooked down with green and red chillies, garlic and a mustard-seed tempering, it becomes gongura pachadi, a thick chutney that keeps for days and is eaten in spoonfuls with rice and ghee. it is also cooked into mutton and prawns, where the acid cuts fat the way vinegar does in a european braise. around it sit the other sours. tamarind is used with a heavier hand here than anywhere except the tamil country, giving pulusu, the stews of fish, brinjal or drumstick that anchor a coastal lunch. ulavacharu, the dark broth left after horse gram is boiled long and slow, is reduced to a sour, smoky, almost meaty liquid and poured over rice. raw mango becomes avakaya, the mustard-and-chilli pickle put down in earthen jars each summer and rationed through the year. curd closes the meal and cools it. sour, salt and heat, in that order, are the andhra signature. chilli is what visitors notice. sour is what the cooks are actually building around, and it is the reason the food works. rice, pappu and the powders on the side the everyday meal on the coast is rice in quantity, served in courses off one plate. it opens with mudda pappu, plain toor dal mashed with nothing more than salt, eaten with ghee and a smear of pickle. then comes a pappu cooked with a vegetable or a sour fruit, tomato, sorrel or the pale dosakaya cucumber; then a dry koora; then pulusu; then charu, the thin peppery broth that is the andhra rasam; and finally curd rice. the sequence moves from rich to light and is closer to a fixed grammar than a menu. between those courses sit the podis, dry powders of roasted lentils, sesame, coconut or curry leaf blitzed with chilli and garlic. kandi podi, made from toor dal, is the common one; there are versions built on peanuts, on gunpowder-hot dried chilli, on dried shrimp along the coast. mixed into hot rice with ghee, a podi is a complete course requiring no cooking at all, which is exactly why it exists: it travels, it keeps without refrigeration, and it turns leftover rice into a meal. the same instinct produces the state's tiffin repertoire, pesarattu ground from whole green gram rather than the usual rice-and-urad batter, punugulu fried from leftover idli batter, upma folded inside the crepe in the godavari districts. three regions, and the millet country inland andhra food is not one food. coastal andhra, watered by the krishna and godavari deltas, is the rice belt and the richest of the three: prawns, freshwater and sea fish, coconut, and a slightly gentler hand with chilli. rayalaseema, the dry interior around kurnool, kadapa and anantapur, is drought country, and its cooking is leaner, hotter and more meat-forward, with natu kodi, the tough country chicken, and ragi sangati, balls of finger millet and rice eaten with a fiery gravy. telangana, on the deccan plateau and a separate state since 2014, has its own kitchen again: jonna rotte and sajja rotte of jowar and bajra, sarva pindi, sakinalu at festival time, and a heavy use of tamarind and sesame. that inland belt was millet country long before it was rice country. jowar, bajra and ragi suited thin soils and an unreliable monsoon, and rice only displaced them across much of the region after the big irrigation projects of the twentieth century filled the canals. the older grains never entirely left, and they are returning now on health and drought-resilience arguments. one kitchen inside this territory belongs to none of the three: the food of hyderabad, shaped by the qutb shahi and asaf jahi courts and by persian and mughal influence, is a deccan court cuisine with its own history, and we treat it separately on the hyderabadi page. quick facts region andhra pradesh and telangana, the eastern deccan and its coast staple grain rice in the deltas; jowar, bajra and ragi inland defining technique dry-roasted spice podis; souring with tamarind, gongura and horse gram broth key ingredient guntur chilli signature protein prawns and river fish on the coast, country chicken and mutton inland, toor dal everywhere pesarattu: ground from whole green gram rather than rice batter, and eaten with ginger chutney. chicken fried down dry with curry leaves, peanuts and a heavy hand of red chilli. signature dishes gongura pachadi : sour roselle leaves cooked

entries.title: Anglo-Indian Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Anglo-Indian cuisine: a community cuisine without a territory, built in the railway colonies of Kharagpur, Jamalpur and Perambur, from mulligatawny and kedgeree to ball curry and the Christmas kalkals.
entries.text: anglo-indian cuisine anglo-indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of anglo-indian cuisine: a community cuisine without a territory, built in the railway colonies of kharagpur, jamalpur and perambur, from mulligatawny and kedgeree to ball curry and the christmas kalkals. anglo-indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana a community, not a region anglo-indian cuisine the one indian cuisine with no territory behind it: a kitchen carried by a people, built along the railway line, and cooked in calcutta and madras rather than in any state. a people, not a place anglo-indians are a distinct community of mixed british and indian descent, descended in the male line from european fathers and indian mothers over some four centuries of portuguese, dutch and then british presence. they are not a colonial footnote and not a historical curiosity: they are a living indian community with their own english-speaking households, schools, churches, associations and, very much, their own food. the constitution names them directly. article 366(2) defines who an anglo-indian is, articles 331 and 333 provided for nominated seats in the lok sabha and in state assemblies, and articles 336 and 337 dealt with their place in the public services and with grants to their schools. frank anthony led the all india anglo-indian association for more than half a century and argued their case in parliament through the whole of that period. the nominated seats lapsed in january 2020 under the 104th amendment; the community did not. what the community has never had is a territory, and that is why anglo-indian food has no zone on khaana's map. every other cuisine on this site can be drawn as a shape — a river plain, a coastline, a plateau, a former court's hinterland. this one cannot. it is a community cuisine, defined by who cooked it rather than where, and it travelled wherever its people were posted. the single attempt to give it ground was mccluskieganj, founded in 1933 in what is now jharkhand by ernest timothy mccluskie as an anglo-indian homeland of a few hundred bungalows. it never held. the cuisine stayed portable instead, which turned out to suit it. the railway colonies from the middle of the nineteenth century the railways, and alongside them the telegraph, the customs service and the post, recruited anglo-indians heavily as drivers, firemen, guards, telegraphists and workshop foremen. the effect was to gather a scattered community into a small number of dense, self-contained settlements. jamalpur in bihar, where the east indian railway opened its workshops in 1862, became the oldest and most storied of them. kharagpur in bengal grew around the bengal nagpur railway workshops from 1900 and had, at its height, one of the largest anglo-indian populations anywhere. perambur in madras did the same in the south. each had its railway institute, its dance floor, its band, its bakery and its own way of doing christmas. the food came out of that arrangement directly. railway quarters had european-style kitchens with ovens and roasting tins, ration books that ran to beef, bread, tinned goods and vinegar, and cooks working an indian spice box inside a british method. men worked shifts and ate on the line, so dishes were built to sit and to reheat, and the pantry favoured what kept: pepper, vinegar, worcestershire sauce, tinned milk and coconut milk. railway mutton curry is the clearest example — a mild, tamarind-sharpened, coconut-loosened curry developed for dining cars and for passengers who wanted spice within limits, cooked down far enough that a day's travel would not spoil it. every other cuisine here can be drawn as a shape on a map. this one is drawn along a railway line, and it goes wherever its people go. the dishes and their double names anglo-indian dishes tend to carry two histories in one name. mulligatawny is the tamil milagu thanni , pepper water, a thin peppery tamarind broth of the kind still drunk over plain rice in tamil households; the british heard a soup where there had been a rasam, and the dish was rebuilt with toor dal, shredded chicken, a spoon of rice and sometimes cream, to be served in a bowl at the start of a meal. kedgeree ran the other way. it began as khichdi, rice and lentils, and returned to britain as a breakfast of rice, flaked smoked fish and chopped boiled egg — an indian dish that emigrated and stayed emigrated. country captain is chicken dry-fried into browned onion and whole red chillies with almost no gravy, its name most likely from the country captains, the skippers of country-built ships trading out of the indian ports. then there is the sunday food. ball curry is beef or mutton meatballs poached in a thin red coconut gravy, eaten with yellow coconut rice — turmeric-gold, steamed in coconut milk with whole spice — and it is the dish anglo-indians of calcutta name first when asked what home tastes like. cutlets and croquettes are the other signature: spiced mince flattened into patties or rolled into fingers, crumbed and shallow-fried until the coating shatters, the technique wholly european and the seasoning wholly indian. devilled dishes, pepper-water, jhal frezi built from cold roast meat, pish pash, and the vinegary chutneys and pickles that came from the same pantry fill out a table that was never a compromise between two cuisines so much as a third thing made by people who belonged to both. calcutta, madras and the christmas table two cities anchored the cuisine, and they cooked differently. calcutta — bow barracks, ripon street, elliot road, and behind them the kharagpur and jamalpur lines — is the beef-eating, ball-curry, christmas-baking centre, with a bakery culture of its own and a strong overlap with the city's armenian and portuguese-descended families. madras, centred on perambur and vepery, sits closer to its tamil ground: more pepper water, more coconut, more rice, mulligatawny that has not travelled as far from milagu thanni. bangalore, secunderabad, nagpur and mhow each held smaller versions of the same pattern around their cantonments and workshops. christmas is when the whole repertoire comes out at once. the sweet tray is the fixed part of it: kalkals, little ridged curls of coconut-milk dough rolled off the back of a for

entries.title: Awadhi / Lucknowi Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Awadhi cuisine: the Nawabs of Oudh, the dum pukht slow-cooking technique, and the legend behind Lucknow's melt-in-the-mouth galouti kebab.
entries.text: awadhi / lucknowi cuisine awadhi/lucknowi cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of awadhi cuisine: the nawabs of oudh, the dum pukht slow-cooking technique, and the legend behind lucknow's melt-in-the-mouth galouti kebab. awadhi/lucknowi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana nawabi north awadhi / lucknowi cuisine the refined court cooking of the nawabs of oudh. sealed-pot slow cooking, gentle spicing, and kebabs made to dissolve on the tongue. a cuisine built for a court, not a marketplace awadhi cuisine takes its name from awadh (oudh), the region around lucknow ruled by the nawabs of oudh from the early 18th century until the british annexed it in 1856. the nawabs began as mughal provincial governors. as central mughal authority weakened, they became independent rulers in practice while keeping mughal court culture, including its cooking, as their model. what developed in lucknow's royal kitchens over the following century was less about heat or heavy spicing than about refinement. technique and aroma mattered more than raw chili, and the cooking was aimed at an audience of one, the nawab, rather than a marketplace of customers. dum pukht and a famine-relief legend dum pukht, literally "breath-cooking," is the defining awadhi technique. meat and rice are sealed into a heavy pot, often with a rim of dough, and cooked slowly over a low, steady fire, so the dish finishes in its own trapped steam and aroma rather than direct heat. lucknow legend ties its popularization to a famine around 1784, when nawab asaf-ud-daula commissioned the bara imambara as a relief-work project. food for the laborers was reportedly cooked overnight in huge sealed deghs (cauldrons) so it would be ready whenever a shift ended. whether or not that story is literally true, it captures what the technique was built for. this is cooking that holds its quality over long, unpredictable stretches of time. "dum pukht" literally means "breath-cooking." the food finishes in its own trapped steam inside a sealed pot, not over open heat. galouti kebab: built for a nawab who had lost his teeth lucknow's best-known dish has a similarly specific legend behind it. the galouti kebab ("melt-in-the-mouth" kebab) is said to have been created for an aging nawab, often identified as asaf-ud-daula or wajid ali shah, who loved kebabs but had lost his teeth. the cooks pounded the meat exceptionally fine and worked in a complex spice blend, popularly (if probably apocryphally) said to run to over a hundred spices. the result was a kebab soft enough to need no chewing at all. lucknow's tunday kebabi, named for its founder's tunda (disabled arm), still trades on a version of that closely guarded recipe today. biryani, the awadhi way awadhi biryani is usually cooked pukki style. the rice and meat are parboiled and cooked separately, then layered and finished together under dum. that gives a drier, more distinctly layered result than hyderabad's kacchi biryani, where raw marinated meat and raw rice go into the pot together from the start. the two techniques, developed in two different nawabi courts, remain the clearest fault line in indian biryani-making. awadhi cooking also travelled well beyond lucknow. when the british exiled the last nawab, wajid ali shah, to calcutta in 1856, he brought his court cooks with him. bengal's own kolkata-style biryani, distinguished by the addition of potato, is usually traced to that exiled awadhi kitchen adapting to leaner circumstances. quick facts region awadh, central-northern uttar pradesh (capital: lucknow) staple grain wheat and rice defining technique dum (sealed slow-cooking) and finely pounded meat key historical moment semi-independent rule by the nawabs of oudh, 18th century to 1856 signature dish galouti kebab galouti kebab: finely pounded, richly spiced meat, designed to need no chewing at all. nihari: a slow-simmered meat stew, traditionally served for breakfast. signature dishes galouti kebab : finely pounded, heavily spiced kebab, said to have been created for a toothless nawab. recipe → lucknowi (pukki) dum biryani : rice and meat parboiled separately, layered, then finished under dum. recipe → nihari : a slow-simmered meat stew, traditionally a breakfast dish. recipe → sheermal : a mildly sweet, saffron-tinted flatbread. recipe → zarda : sweet saffron rice, often served to close a meal. recipe → recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian meal.

entries.title: Bengali Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Bengali cuisine: river fish, mustard oil, and the invention of rosogolla in 19th-century Kolkata.
entries.text: bengali cuisine bengali cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of bengali cuisine: river fish, mustard oil, and the invention of rosogolla in 19th-century kolkata. bengali cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana east india bengali cuisine a rice and fish delta cuisine with a sweet tooth precise enough to be its own art form. a cuisine built by a river delta bengal sits on the ganges-brahmaputra delta, one of the most fertile and water-rich regions on earth, and its food reflects that directly. rice is the staple, and freshwater and river fish (hilsa/ilish above all) are the main protein. mustard grows across bengal's fields and supplies both the seeds for pungent mustard-paste sauces and the oil that bengali cooking is built on. where punjab cooks in ghee, bengal cooks in mustard oil, and that difference defines the cuisine as much as any spice does. a meal with a structure a traditional bengali meal isn't served all at once. it moves through courses in a set order. it starts with something bitter (shukto, a mixed-vegetable dish) to wake up the palate, then rice and dal, then a vegetable dish, then fish or meat curry, then chutney, and finally something sweet. that's closer to a french tasting menu than to the single-plate thali found across most of the rest of india. the meal is paced as a sequence rather than assembled on one plate. where most of india treats sweets as dessert, bengal treats them as a technical discipline in their own right. the invention of rosogolla bengali sweets stand apart because of one technique. cooks curdle milk into chhena (fresh cheese) and shape it into desserts, which is unusual in indian sweet-making. most of the rest of the country relies on reduced milk (khoya) or dough instead. the most famous result, rosogolla (spongy chhena balls in sugar syrup), is credited to kolkata confectioner nobin chandra das around 1868. some food historians trace the cheese-curdling method back further, to portuguese traders and missionaries who brought cheese-making to bengal centuries earlier. that makes rosogolla a 19th-century bengali invention built on a much older imported technique. sandesh, a firmer chhena sweet often flavored with jaggery, developed alongside it as the other pillar of bengali confectionery. calcutta and colonial-era influence as the capital of british india until 1911, calcutta had more direct contact with european cooking than most indian cities of its time. anglo-indian dishes, western-style cutlets and chops, and a citywide restaurant and confectionery culture all grew out of this period. they layered onto the older rice-fish-mustard base of home cooking. quick facts region west bengal (and historically undivided bengal) staple grain rice defining technique mustard oil & mustard-paste cooking; chhena (fresh cheese) sweets key historical moment rosogolla's invention in 1860s kolkata signature protein freshwater & river fish, especially hilsa (ilish) rosogolla (rasgulla): spongy chhena balls in sugar syrup, invented in 1860s kolkata. shorshe ilish: hilsa fish cooked in a pungent mustard-seed paste. signature dishes machher jhol : a light, everyday fish curry. recipe → shorshe ilish : hilsa fish in mustard sauce, arguably bengal's most iconic dish. recipe → kosha mangsho : a slow-cooked, dark, richly spiced mutton curry. recipe → rosogolla (rasgulla) : spongy chhena balls in sugar syrup. recipe → sandesh : a firmer chhena sweet, often flavored with jaggery. recipe → mishti doi : sweetened, slow-fermented yogurt. recipe → recipes based on entries.title: Bihari Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Bihari cuisine: sattu as everyday protein, litti chokha baked over embers, the Magadha and Mithila kitchens, and the sweets of Gaya, Silao and Maner.
entries.text: bihari cuisine bihari cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of bihari cuisine: sattu as everyday protein, litti chokha baked over embers, the magadha and mithila kitchens, and the sweets of gaya, silao and maner. bihari cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana east india bihari cuisine a gangetic plain cuisine built on roasted gram, mustard oil and live embers, feeding more people on less than almost any kitchen in india. sattu, the flour that does the work of meat if one ingredient explains bihar, it is sattu: chana roasted whole and then stone-ground into a nutty, high-protein flour. it needs no cooking, keeps for weeks without refrigeration, and costs very little. that combination made it the everyday protein of a densely populated, largely agricultural state, and it turns up in almost every meal. whisked into cold water with black salt, lemon and green chilli it becomes sattu sharbat, drunk by the glass through a bihari summer. spiked with garlic, ajwain and mustard oil it stuffs parathas and litti. the rest of the pantry is the gangetic plain's: wheat and rice, mustard oil pressed sharp, panch phoran for the tempering, and freshwater fish from the ganga, gandak and kosi. bihari cooking is not subtle in the way awadhi cooking next door is subtle. it is direct, sour with lemon and amchur, hot with raw mustard oil and green chilli, and it leans on smoke and char rather than long-simmered gravies. litti chokha, and cooking without a stove litti is a ball of wheat dough packed with seasoned sattu and baked hard in the ashes of a cow-dung or coal fire, then cracked open and drowned in ghee. chokha, its partner, is roasted brinjal, tomato and potato mashed with raw onion, mustard oil and lemon. the pairing is the state's best-known dish, and its logic is the logic of field food: it needs no pan, no stove and no gravy, it travels, and it keeps. that ember-baked technique gave bihar a reputation as poor food, which it has spent the last two decades shedding. litti chokha now turns up in patna restaurants and delhi food halls, and the dish has become a marker of bihari identity well beyond the state. litti needs no pan, no stove and no gravy. it is field food that outlived the field, and it now carries a state's name. magadha, mithila, and two different kitchens bihar is not one food region. the south and centre — old magadha, with pataliputra at its heart, the seat of the mauryan empire and the ground on which both buddhism and jainism took shape — leans vegetarian, wheat-heavy and austere. the north, across the ganga, is mithila: the maithil brahmin and kayastha kitchens of darbhanga and madhubani, where fish is everyday food rather than an exception, and rice displaces wheat. a maithil wedding feast and a magadhi one look very different. the northwest has its own claim. champaran, on the nepal border, gave india ahuna mutton — meat, mustard oil, garlic and whole spices sealed inside an earthen handi with dough and cooked slowly over its own steam, the pot broken open at the table. it is the one bihari dish that is unapologetically rich. sweets with addresses bihari sweets are unusually place-specific: each belongs to a named town and is judged against it. silao, near nalanda, makes khaja, a layered fried pastry soaked in syrup that carries a geographical indication tag. gaya makes tilkut, sesame and jaggery pounded together by hand in winter workshops for makar sankranti. maner makes laddus. thekua, ridged wheat biscuits fried in ghee, are made for chhath, the four-day festival of the sun god that is the most important date in the bihari calendar and whose offerings are cooked under strict rules of purity. the state's newest recognition is agricultural rather than culinary. mithila makhana — foxnut, popped from the seeds of a water lily grown in north bihar's ponds — received a gi tag in 2022, and the crop has become one of the region's few genuine export successes. quick facts region bihar and jharkhand, the middle gangetic plain staple grain wheat in the south and centre, rice in mithila defining technique ember-baking; sattu fillings; panch phoran tempering in raw mustard oil key ingredient sattu, roasted gram flour signature protein freshwater fish, mutton, gram and pulses champaran ahuna mutton: sealed in an earthen handi with dough and cooked in its own steam. tilkut being pounded by hand in gaya, made through the winter for makar sankranti. signature dishes litti chokha : sattu-stuffed wheat balls baked in embers, dipped in ghee and crushed over smoky mashed vegetables. recipe → sattu ka paratha : flatbread stuffed with roasted gram flour, garlic, ajwain and mustard oil. recipe → sattu sharbat : roasted gram flour whisked into cold water with black salt, lemon and green chilli. recipe → champaran ahuna mutton : mutton slow-cooked in a dough-sealed earthen handi. chana ghugni : black or white gram simmered dry and finished with onion, lemon and chilli. recipe → dal pitha : steamed rice-flour dumplings stuffed with spiced chana dal. recipe → kadhi bari : gram-flour dumplings in a sour, turmeric-yellow buttermilk gravy. recipe → thekua : ridged wheat-and-jaggery biscuits fried in ghee, made for chhath. recipe → khaja : layered fried pastry in syrup, tied to the town of silao. recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, entries.title: Goan Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Goan cuisine: 450 years of Portuguese rule, the origin of vindaloo, and the Hindu-Catholic culinary split.
entries.text: goan cuisine goan cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of goan cuisine: 450 years of portuguese rule, the origin of vindaloo, and the hindu-catholic culinary split. goan cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana coastal india goan cuisine 450 years of portuguese rule, folded into a konkani coastal tradition and preserved in the name of a single dish. the longest colonial presence in india goa was a portuguese colony from 1510 until 1961, roughly 450 years. that makes it by far the longest continuous european colonial presence anywhere in india (british rule, by comparison, lasted under 200 years). the length mattered. it gave portuguese ingredients and techniques time to genuinely integrate into local cooking rather than sit alongside it. the result is a cuisine that is authentically both konkani coastal and portuguese-iberian at once, rather than one simply borrowing from the other. vindaloo's name is a history lesson the clearest evidence is sitting in plain sight in the name of goa's best-known dish. vindaloo derives from the portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos , meat marinated in wine ( vinho ) and garlic ( alhos ). that was a preservation technique portuguese sailors used for meat on long sea voyages. in goa, wine vinegar was often substituted or supplemented with local palm vinegar, garlic remained central, and chili (a portuguese-introduced new world import) was added. a shipboard preservation method had become one of india's most recognizable curries. the dish's name is, essentially, a 500-year-old linguistic fossil. vindaloo's name literally means "meat, wine, and garlic" in portuguese. the recipe is a shipboard preservation trick that became a national dish. two goan cuisines, split by religion goa's food culture, like rajasthan's, really contains two distinct traditions, here split along religious lines. goan catholic cuisine, from the community most directly shaped by portuguese conversion and rule, centers on pork, beef, and vinegar-based dishes like vindaloo and sorpotel, alongside portuguese-derived desserts like bebinca, a rich layered coconut-and-egg cake. goan hindu cuisine, particularly that of the saraswat brahmins, stayed closer to the broader konkani coastal tradition, built on fish, coconut, and kokum, with far less portuguese influence and no pork or beef. both are unambiguously goan. they simply come from different communities within the same 450-year colonial history. cashews, chilies, and the wider ripple effect goa's port role also made it one of the entry points through which new world crops first reached the indian subcontinent, among them chilies, potatoes, tomatoes, and cashews, carried in on portuguese trade routes after 1510. from there they spread into the rest of indian cooking over the following centuries. the cashew took root so successfully in goa's soil that it is now used to distill feni, the region's signature spirit. quick facts entries.title: Gujarati Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Gujarati cuisine: Jain vegetarianism, maritime trade, and the sweet-salty-sour balance of the Gujarati thali.
entries.text: gujarati cuisine gujarati cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of gujarati cuisine: jain vegetarianism, maritime trade, and the sweet-salty-sour balance of the gujarati thali. gujarati cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana west india gujarati cuisine india's great vegetarian tradition, where sweet, salty, and sour are balanced deliberately on a single plate. trade, religion, and a coastline gujarat has been a maritime trading region since antiquity. lothal, one of the indus valley civilization's key port cities, sat on gujarat's coast, and the port of surat became one of the mughal empire's busiest trade hubs by the 17th century. that history brought early, sustained contact with outside ingredients and cultures. the more decisive influence on the cuisine, though, is religious. gujarat has one of india's largest jain populations, and jain dietary law prohibits root vegetables as well as meat, to avoid harming the organisms in the soil. that pushed the region toward one of the subcontinent's oldest and most disciplined vegetarian traditions. the sweet-salty-sour thali the defining trait of gujarati cooking, more than any single ingredient, is a deliberate balancing act. many savory dishes carry a small amount of sugar or jaggery alongside chili and tamarind or lemon, so a single dish, and a full thali, moves between sweet, salty, sour, and spicy rather than settling on one note. that is not inconsistency. it is a codified aesthetic, and one of the more instantly identifiable regional signatures in indian cooking, since most other regions treat sweetness strictly as a dessert category. a pinch of sugar in the dal isn't a mistake in gujarati cooking. it's the whole point. farsan, and food built for trade routes gujarat also produced one of india's richest snack-food traditions, known as farsan. these are steamed, fried, or fermented savory snacks like dhokla and khandvi, most built from besan (gram flour) or fermented rice-lentil batters. farsan developed partly as travel food for a historically mercantile, road-and-sea-trading population, favoring items that kept well and travelled easily. that same trading community, the gujarati and marwari merchant diaspora, later carried gujarati vegetarian food culture across india and eventually the world, making dishes like dhokla recognizable well outside the state. quick facts region western india (gujarat) staple grain wheat & millet (bajra, jowar), plus rice on the coast defining technique sweet-salty-sour balancing; steamed & fried gram-flour snacks (farsan) key historical influence jain vegetarianism & a long maritime trading history signature trait one of india's most strictly vegetarian regional cuisines dhokla: a steamed, fermented gram-flour cake. undhiyu: a slow-cooked mixed-vegetable dish, a surat winter specialty. signature dishes dhokla : a steamed, spongy, fermented gram-flour cake. recipe → khandvi : thin, rolled gram-flour and yogurt savory bites. recipe → undhiyu : a slow-cooked mix of winter vegetables, a surat specialty. recipe → thepla : a spiced flatbread, often made with fenugreek leaves. recipe → fafda-jalebi : crisp gram-flour strips paired with a syrup-soaked sweet, a classic weekend breakfast. recipe → gujarati kadhi : a mildly sweetened yogurt-and-gram-flour soup. recipe → recipes based on entries.title: Himachali & Pahari Cuisine
entries.snippet: The hill cooking of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand: the dham feast and its yogurt madras, Kumaoni and Garhwali pulses and millets, and a pantry built for winter.
entries.text: himachali & pahari cuisine himachali & pahari cuisine: history & iconic dishes the hill cooking of himachal pradesh and uttarakhand: the dham feast and its yogurt madras, kumaoni and garhwali pulses and millets, and a pantry built for winter. himachali & pahari cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana the himalaya himachali & pahari cuisine hill cooking built for winter: dried pulses, soured yogurt gravies, coarse mountain grains, and feasts served on leaf plates by hereditary cooks. a pantry built for six months of snow pahari cooking — the food of the himalayan hills — is shaped less by what grows than by what survives. above about six thousand feet the growing season is short, the passes close, and for months the only vegetables available are the ones dried in autumn and strung from a beam. so the hill kitchen learned to build meals out of stores: black gram and kidney beans, horse gram and black soybean, dried apricots, sun-dried greens, fermented bamboo in the eastern hills, and grains that ripen fast at altitude. fresh produce is a summer luxury, not the foundation. two consequences follow. the first is that pulses do the heavy lifting: a pahari meal is more likely to be built around a dal than around a vegetable, and the dals are dense, dark and slow. the second is that sourness has to be manufactured rather than picked. yogurt, buttermilk, dried mango powder, tamarind and locally the sharp wild fruits of the hills all stand in for the citrus and tomatoes a plains kitchen takes for granted. that single constraint — sour from a jar, not from a tree — explains a surprising amount of what follows. the dham, and the men who cook it himachal's great communal meal is the dham, served at weddings, temple festivals and village gatherings. guests sit in long rows on the floor and eat from pattals, plates stitched from leaves, while the food comes down the line in buckets. it is cooked not by the household but by botis — hereditary cooks, in himachal usually brahmins, who inherit the job and the recipes from their fathers and who begin work the night before over wood fires and enormous brass vessels. a single boti and his team may feed a thousand people from one courtyard. the dham has a fixed grammar. rice first, then a dal, then the madras: gravies thickened with whisked yogurt, gently soured and barely spiced with anything hot, in which chickpeas or kidney beans are simmered until they take on the tang. sepu vadi, fried lentil cakes sunk into a dark dal, appears in the kangra version. the meal ends in khatta and then mitha — something sour, then something sweet, usually a sweet rice. nothing is fried at the table and nothing is served hot off a tandoor; the whole structure is designed to be cooked in bulk hours ahead and still taste right. yogurt is the hill cook's tomato: the thing that makes a gravy taste of something when nothing fresh is in season. across the watershed: kumaon and garhwal himachal pradesh and uttarakhand are separate states with separate histories — uttarakhand was carved out of uttar pradesh only in 2000 — but their hill cooking rhymes so closely that it makes little sense to treat them apart, which is why they share a page here. uttarakhand's two halves, kumaon in the east and garhwal in the west, cook on the same logic of stored pulses and coarse grains, with their own vocabulary. gahat, horse gram, is the regional obsession: hard, warming, credited with dissolving kidney stones, and cooked into thick dals and into ras, a soupy pulse broth poured over rice. bhatt, the black soybean, becomes churkani, thickened with a spoonful of toasted flour. the grains are different too. jhangora, barnyard millet, and mandua, finger millet, ripen where rice and wheat will not, and both remain everyday food rather than a health-shop revival: mandua goes into dark rotis, jhangora into a milky kheer. garhwal's own signatures are chainsoo, black gram roasted before grinding until the dal turns almost black and smells of woodsmoke, and phaanu, several soaked pulses ground together and cooked to a loose, soupy dal. these are dishes engineered for calories and warmth at altitude, and they taste like it. mustard oil, hing, and the missing onion the fat is mustard oil, pressed sharp and heated to smoking before anything goes into it, though ghee appears at feasts and in the kangra valley's richer cooking. the spicing is restrained by plains standards: hing, cumin, coriander, turmeric, a little garam masala, and in uttarakhand jakhiya, a wild mustard-family seed that pops like a cross between mustard and nigella and is used almost exclusively in these hills. chillies are present but rarely dominant; heat is not what pahari food is for. the most conspicuous absence is onion and garlic. in much pahari brahmin cooking, and in the dham and temple food especially, both are simply not used — a dietary rule shared with several other indian brahmin traditions, which treats them as agitating foods unsuited to ritual purity. hing does the work instead, providing the savoury base note that alliums would otherwise supply. it is worth noting because it explains the flavour: a madra or a chainsoo tastes the way it does partly because of what has been left out, and the technique of building depth from yogurt, toasted spice and long cooking developed to fill that gap. quick facts region himachal pradesh and uttarakhand, the western himalayan hills staple grain rice and wheat in the valleys; mandua and jhangora millets higher up defining technique yogurt-thickened madra gravies; pulses roasted before grinding; slow wood-fire cooking in bulk key ingredient yogurt, with hing and mustard oil in place of onion and garlic signature protein dried pulses — black gram, rajma, gahat and bhatt; goat at feasts signature dishes siddu : yeasted wheat bread steamed over a pot, stuffed with walnuts or spiced pulses and eaten with ghee. recipe → chana madra : chickpeas simmered in a whisked yogurt gravy with whole spices and no onion or garlic. recipe → sepu vadi : fried urad lentil cakes sunk into a dark spinach and dal gravy, a kangra dham centrepiece. recipe → entries.title: Hyderabadi Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Hyderabadi cuisine: the Nizams' court kitchens, the Qutb Shahi dynasty, and the dum technique behind Hyderabadi biryani.
entries.text: hyderabadi cuisine hyderabadi cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of hyderabadi cuisine: the nizams' court kitchens, the qutb shahi dynasty, and the dum technique behind hyderabadi biryani. hyderabadi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana the deccan hyderabadi cuisine persian court cooking met telugu spice tradition here. four centuries in the making, with one dish at the center of it all. two dynasties, one fusion cuisine hyderabadi cuisine is a fusion in the most literal sense. its history is unusually well documented because it grew up as a court cuisine, shaped deliberately by ruling dynasties rather than by agriculture and geography alone. the qutb shahi dynasty, which ruled the golconda sultanate from the 16th to 17th century, brought persian court cooking to the deccan. when the mughal empire later absorbed the region and the nizams (the asaf jahi dynasty) took power in the 18th century, their kitchens combined that persian-mughal foundation with the spice-forward telugu and marathwada cooking already established locally. the result is rich and fragrant on its persian-mughal side and sharply spiced on its deccan side. the dum technique what sets hyderabadi biryani apart from other indian biryanis is the cooking method rather than the spice blend. in the "kachi" (raw) style, marinated raw meat is layered directly with partially cooked rice. the pot is sealed and slow-cooked over low heat (dum), so the rice finishes cooking in the steam and juices the meat releases. the two are never cooked separately and combined afterward. this layering-and-sealing method, often done by sealing the lid with dough to trap steam, came from persian court kitchens. its survival in hyderabad is a direct trace of the nizams' persian-influenced cooks. the layering-and-sealing technique behind hyderabadi biryani is a 300-year-old persian court method, still practiced almost exactly as it was. haleem and the nizami table haleem, a dense, slow-pounded stew of wheat, lentils, and meat, has similarly deep roots. it traces back to arab and persian meat-and-wheat porridges (related to the middle eastern harees), brought into the nizams' kitchens and adapted with local spice. in hyderabad it is now tied closely to ramadan, served as an iftar dish across the city each evening during the fasting month. quick facts region deccan plateau (hyderabad, telangana) staple grain rice defining technique dum: sealed-pot, layered slow-cooking key historical influence qutb shahi & nizami (asaf jahi) court kitchens, 16th to 20th century signature dish hyderabadi biryani haleem: a slow-pounded wheat, lentil, and meat stew with roots in arab and persian cooking. qubani ka meetha: a stewed apricot dessert of persian dessert lineage, served with cream. signature dishes hyderabadi biryani : layered, dum-cooked rice and marinated meat. recipe → haleem : a slow-pounded wheat, lentil, and meat stew, a ramadan specialty. recipe → mirchi ka salan : a tangy chili curry in a peanut-sesame gravy. recipe → double ka meetha : a bread pudding fried and soaked in sweetened milk, of persian dessert lineage. recipe → qubani ka meetha : a stewed apricot dessert, served with cream. recipe → recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian meal.

entries.title: Karnataka Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Karnataka cuisine: ragi and jowar as the real inland staples, the Udupi temple kitchens that exported the dosa across India, Mangalorean seafood, and the pork and kachampuli of Coorg.
entries.text: karnataka cuisine karnataka cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of karnataka cuisine: ragi and jowar as the real inland staples, the udupi temple kitchens that exported the dosa across india, mangalorean seafood, and the pork and kachampuli of coorg. karnataka cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana south india karnataka cuisine three kitchens under one name: millet in the dry interior, coconut and fish on the coast, and the temple cooking that put the dosa on every high street in india. three karnatakas, not one the state that exists today was assembled in 1956 out of territory that had been mysore princely state, bombay presidency, madras presidency, the nizam's hyderabad and the coorg province. the kitchens never merged. southern karnataka, the old mysore heartland around mandya, hassan and bengaluru, eats finger millet and rice with mild coconut-and-dal gravies. north karnataka — vijayapura, bagalkot, dharwad, kalaburagi — is a jowar belt that cooks with groundnut, dry chilli and sesame and looks far more like the maharashtrian deccan than like mysore. the coastal strip, udupi and dakshina kannada, is a wet, coconut-heavy seafood country with its own languages. the kannada vocabulary of the table is worth knowing because it maps the differences. saaru is the thin peppery broth that elsewhere is rasam; huli is the thicker tamarind-and-dal stew that elsewhere is sambar; palya is a dry vegetable stir-fry; bath covers the one-pot rice dishes. the same four words appear across the state, but a dharwad saaru and a udupi saaru share almost nothing beyond the name. the udupi kitchens that exported the dosa udupi's krishna matha was founded by the philosopher madhvacharya in the thirteenth century, and the eight monasteries around it — the ashta mathas — take turns running the temple in a rotation handed over at the paryaya festival every two years. feeding pilgrims at that scale, every day, under strict sattvic rules that bar onion and garlic, forced the temple cooks into genuine invention. the shivalli brahmin families who staffed those kitchens built a repertoire of rice-and-lentil batters, coconut-ground gravies and vegetable dishes that could be cooked in volume, served fast and eaten by anyone. from the late nineteenth century those families began leaving for bombay and madras, where they opened cheap, clean, vegetarian eating houses. the udupi hotel became a category of its own: marble tables, a menu of idli, vada, dosa and coffee, and food that observant customers of any caste could eat without anxiety. chains like woodlands and dasaprakash carried the format nationwide, and by the middle of the twentieth century the dosa had stopped being a regional dish and become the default indian breakfast in cities that had never heard of udupi. mysore added its own version — the masala dosa smeared inside with red chilli-garlic chutney. the dosa did not travel on its own merits. it travelled with the cooks of eight monasteries, who needed food that anyone could eat. ragi and jowar, the grains under the rice restaurant karnataka runs on rice; the countryside largely does not. across the dry southern maidan, the staple is ragi — finger millet — cooked into ragi mudde, dense balls swallowed rather than chewed, with a bowl of soppu saaru, bassaru or country chicken curry alongside. ragi grows on poor soil with unreliable rain, keeps well, and delivers far more calcium and iron than polished rice. karnataka still grows more of it than any other indian state. north of the krishna, the grain changes to jowar. jolada rotti, a thin unleavened sorghum bread dry-toasted until it puffs and then stacked to go stiff, is the daily bread of vijayapura and bagalkot, eaten with stuffed brinjal, jhunka and fierce chutney powders ground from dry chilli, garlic and groundnut. rice-flour akki rotti, patted straight onto the tawa with onion and dill, sits between the two. millet was called poor-man's food for most of the twentieth century and pushed aside by subsidised rice; the last decade has reversed the snobbery entirely, and ragi and jowar now sell at a premium in the same cities that dropped them. the coast and the hills dakshina kannada cooks in at least three traditions at once. the tulu-speaking bunts gave the coast kori rotti, a fiery chicken curry poured over brittle rice wafers that soften as you eat them. the konkani-speaking gowd saraswat brahmins, a fish-eating brahmin community, contributed the gentler coconut-and-tamarind curries. mangalorean catholics, descended from goan converts who moved south in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and survived captivity at seringapatam under tipu sultan, brought pork, vinegar and the bafat masala. the unifying ingredients are coconut in every form and the byadgi chilli, grown inland in haveri, which stains a gravy deep red without much heat — the reason kundapur ghee roast looks far angrier than it tastes. inland and up, kodagu — coorg — is a different country again: a hill district of coffee, cardamom and black pepper, and the home of the kodavas, a martial, ancestor-venerating community with no dietary restrictions to speak of. their central dish is pandi curry, pork cooked black with coarse pepper and soured with kachampuli, a thick dark reduction of malabar tamarind that no other indian cuisine uses. it is eaten with steamed rice dumplings — kadambuttu — or with otti, a flat rice bread. coorg cooking is the least exported of karnataka's kitchens and the least changed. quick facts region karnataka, including coastal mangalore and udupi and the hills of coorg staple grain ragi in the south, jowar in the north, rice on the coast defining technique batter fermentation; wet coconut masalas ground on stone; dry-toasted millet breads key ingredient coconut, and the byadgi chilli for colour without heat signature protein lentils inland, seafood on the coast, pork in coorg ragi mudde with country chicken saaru: the everyday plate of the southern maidan, swallowed rather than chewed. neer dosa, poured from an unfermented rice batter thin enough to see through, folded straight off the pan. signature dishes ragi mudde : smooth finger-millet balls, the everyday staple of the southern karnataka plate. recipe → j

entries.title: Kashmiri Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Kashmiri cuisine: Central Asian chefs brought by Timur, the wazwan feast, and the religious split between Kashmiri Pandit and Kashmiri Muslim cooking.
entries.text: kashmiri cuisine kashmiri cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of kashmiri cuisine: central asian chefs brought by timur, the wazwan feast, and the religious split between kashmiri pandit and kashmiri muslim cooking. kashmiri cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana himalayan north kashmiri cuisine a persian-inflected court cuisine grafted onto a himalayan valley, built around a feast that treats meat as ceremony rather than ingredient. a central asian graft onto a himalayan valley kashmiri cooking's most distinctive institution, the wazwan feast, doesn't trace back to the rest of the indian subcontinent at all. its roots are usually placed in the late 14th century, when timur's invasion of kashmir brought central asian and persian cooks, the wazas, into the valley. over the following centuries, under later sultanate and mughal-era patronage, that imported tradition merged with local ingredients (saffron, lotus stem, local lamb). what emerged was no longer quite persian, and no longer quite anything else on the subcontinent either. the wazwan: a feast measured in courses, not dishes a full wazwan traditionally runs to around 36 courses. a team of wazas prepares it, led by a head chef called the vaste waza, and it is served family-style on a single large platter called a trami, four diners to a plate. you cook it for weddings and major occasions rather than ordering it off a menu, and the meal builds toward a defined climax instead of just presenting dishes in sequence. the wazwan's final course is always the same dish: gushtaba, pounded meatballs in a white yogurt gravy. its arrival signals that the feast is over. two kashmiri cuisines, split by religion as in goa and rajasthan, one regional label covers two distinct culinary traditions here, split along religious lines. kashmiri pandit (hindu) cooking avoids onion and garlic on religious grounds and builds its pungency instead from asafoetida (hing) and dried ginger powder (saunth), producing dishes like a pale, tangy pandit-style yakhni. kashmiri muslim cooking, the tradition behind the wazwan, leans heavily on onion and garlic and produces the deep-red rogan josh most outsiders associate with the region. same valley, same core ingredients, genuinely different everyday cooking. saffron, and the valley's one true luxury crop the fields around pampore, near srinagar, are one of the very few places on earth where saffron is grown commercially, and kashmir treats it accordingly. it is a defining flavor here rather than a garnish, turning up in modur pulav (sweet saffron rice) and in desserts. above all it goes into kahwa, a green tea steeped with saffron, cardamom, and almonds and served without milk. that makes it a genuinely different drink from the milk-based chai found almost everywhere else in india. quick facts region kashmir valley (himalayan north) staple grain rice defining technique slow-cooked meat, hand-pounded for hours key historical moment central asian wazas arriving with timur's 14th-century invasion signature dish rogan josh modur pulav: sweet saffron rice studded with dried fruit and nuts. dum aloo: baby potatoes slow-cooked in a spiced, deep-red gravy. signature dishes rogan josh : lamb cooked in oil at high heat, colored deep red by kashmiri chili or, traditionally, ratan jot (cockscomb flower) rather than tomato. recipe → yakhni : a yogurt-based curry cooked with whole spices; the pandit version omits onion, garlic, turmeric, and chili entirely. recipe → gushtaba : hand-pounded meatballs in white yogurt gravy, the ceremonial final course of the wazwan. recipe → modur pulav : sweet saffron rice with dried fruit, milk, and sugar. recipe → kahwa : green tea with saffron, cardamom, and almonds, served without entries.title: Kerala Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Kerala cuisine: the Malabar spice trade that drew Rome, Arabia, China, and Europe to one coastline, coconut as the region's defining fat, and the Onam sadya feast.
entries.text: kerala cuisine kerala cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of kerala cuisine: the malabar spice trade that drew rome, arabia, china, and europe to one coastline, coconut as the region's defining fat, and the onam sadya feast. kerala cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana malabar coast kerala cuisine the coastline that drew rome, arabia, china, and europe in search of a single spice, built around coconut instead of ghee and a religious diversity few other regions can match. the coast the whole world sailed for kerala's food history starts with a fact that's easy to underrate. for close to two thousand years, the malabar coast was the world's main source of black pepper, valuable enough to draw roman traders, arab merchants, and chinese fleets to the same stretch of coastline long before the mughals ever set foot in india. that trade reached its best-known turning point in 1498, when vasco da gama landed at kozhikode (calicut) in search of pepper. his voyage opened a direct european sea route to india, and with it over a century of portuguese and later dutch and british competition for the spice trade. kerala did not merely take part in that history. for a very long time, it was the reason for it. three communities, one coastline centuries of trade left kerala with a religious and culinary diversity that's unusual even within india. kochi has hosted a jewish community since roughly the time of the spice trade's earliest centuries. arab traders left behind the mappila muslim community of the malabar coast, whose thalassery biryani, built on a small-grained khyma rice rather than basmati, is genuinely distinct from both the hyderabadi and awadhi versions. and kerala's syrian christian community, tracing its roots to some of the oldest christian communities outside the middle east, contributes rich, dark meat dishes like duck roast and beef fry that sit alongside an otherwise heavily vegetarian hindu tradition. vasco da gama didn't sail to india in general. he sailed to kozhikode, specifically for kerala's pepper. coconut, not ghee, as the defining fat where punjabi or awadhi cooking runs on ghee and dairy, kerala's kitchens run on coconut in nearly every form at once. coconut oil handles the frying and tempering, thick coconut milk finishes a curry, and fresh grated coconut goes straight into chutneys and vegetable dishes. it suits a tropical, coastal climate, and it is the single clearest thing separating kerala's cooking from its northern neighbors and even from much of the rest of south india. a vegetarian feast from a state famous for its beef kerala is one of the few indian states, alongside goa and the northeast, where beef is commonly and openly eaten, mostly among its large christian and muslim communities. that makes the sadya, kerala's traditional festival feast, a striking contrast. it is an entirely vegetarian meal of around twenty to twenty-six dishes, served in a fixed arrangement on a banana leaf and eaten by hand. it is central to onam and other major celebrations, whatever a household eats the rest of the year. the sadya is less a dinner than a piece of shared choreography, right down to the order in which dishes are mixed into the rice. quick facts region malabar coast, southwest india staple grain rice defining technique coconut oil, milk, and grated coconut used in nearly every dish key historical moment centuries at the center of the global pepper trade, culminating in vasco da gama's 1498 landing at calicut signature dish fish curry meen curry: fish simmered in a tangy, coconut-and-kokum gravy, traditionally cooked in a clay pot. appam with duck curry: a lacy, fermented rice pancake paired with a rich syrian christian specialty. signature dishes meen curry (fish curry) : fish simmered in a tangy coconut gravy, often soured with kokum. recipe → appam : a fermented rice-and-coconut pancake, lacy and thin at the edges, thick in the center. recipe → sadya : a roughly 20-to-26-dish vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf for onam and other celebrations. thalassery biryani : a mappila muslim biryani made with small-grained khyma rice rather than basmati. duck roast : a rich, dark, spice-heavy dish from kerala's syrian christian tradition. recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian entries.title: Maharashtrian Cuisine
entries.snippet: How geography split Maharashtrian cuisine into a coastal Konkan tradition and a spicy Deccan one, and how vada pav was invented for Mumbai's mill workers.
entries.text: maharashtrian cuisine maharashtrian cuisine: history & iconic dishes how geography split maharashtrian cuisine into a coastal konkan tradition and a spicy deccan one, and how vada pav was invented for mumbai's mill workers. maharashtrian cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana west india maharashtrian cuisine a coastal tradition and a plateau tradition, sharing one state, plus the street food that fed mumbai's mill workers. konkan coast vs. deccan plateau maharashtra's cuisine really splits into two distinct traditions defined by geography. along the konkan coast, the food looks a lot like its coastal neighbors goa and kerala: rice, coconut, and seafood, cooked with kokum (a tart dried fruit) for sourness. inland, on the drier deccan plateau, the cuisine shifts to millets (jowar and bajra) instead of rice, peanuts and sesame instead of coconut, and famously dry, intensely spiced curries. kolhapuri cuisine, from the southern deccan, is often cited as one of the spiciest regional styles in india. the maratha empire and a warrior food culture maharashtra's political identity is inseparable from the maratha empire, built under chhatrapati shivaji in the 17th century and expanding into one of the dominant powers in india by the 18th. foods tied to military campaigns had to be practical, portable, and high in energy. dry chutneys, spice mixes like goda masala and kanda-lasun masala, and preserved pickles all fit that need. they stayed in everyday cooking long after the campaigns ended. vada pav wasn't handed down through generations. it was invented on a specific street corner, for a specific economic reason, in 1966. mumbai and the invention of vada pav the most-told food-history story from this region is a recent, well-documented one. vada pav, a spiced potato fritter in a bread roll, is credited to a street vendor named ashok vaidya, who began selling it near dadar railway station in 1966. it was explicitly designed as a cheap, fast, filling meal for mumbai's textile mill workers, at a time when western-style sandwiches were priced out of reach for that same crowd. it's a rare case in indian food history where a genuinely "invented" dish, rather than one that gradually evolved, can be traced to a specific person, place, and year. it went on to become mumbai's defining street food. quick facts region western india (maharashtra): coastal konkan & inland deccan staple grain rice (coastal), jowar & bajra millets (inland) defining technique coconut-and-kokum coastal cooking; dry, intense deccan spice blends key historical moment vada pav's invention near dadar station, mumbai, 1966 signature dish vada pav misal pav: a spicy sprouted-lentil curry topped with farsan, served with bread. modak: a steamed rice-flour dumpling filled with coconut and jaggery. signature dishes vada pav : a spiced potato fritter in a bread roll, invented in mumbai in 1966. recipe → misal pav : a spicy sprouted-lentil curry topped with crunchy farsan, served with bread. recipe → puran poli : a sweet flatbread stuffed with a jaggery-lentil filling. recipe → modak : a steamed dumpling of rice flour, coconut, and jaggery, associated with the ganesh chaturthi festival. recipe → kolhapuri mutton : an intensely spiced, dry-roasted-masala curry from the southern deccan. recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in
