entries.title: Northeast Indian Cuisine
entries.snippet: How isolation from the mainland gave India's eight northeastern states a cuisine built on fermentation and smoking rather than garam masala and dairy.
entries.text: northeast indian cuisine northeast indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes how isolation from the mainland gave india's eight northeastern states a cuisine built on fermentation and smoking rather than garam masala and dairy. northeast indian cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana eight states northeast indian cuisine not one cuisine but eight, connected less to mainland indian cooking than to the fermentation and bamboo traditions of tibet and southeast asia across the border. not one cuisine, but eight "northeast indian" is a geographic label, not a culinary one. it covers assam, arunachal pradesh, manipur, meghalaya, mizoram, nagaland, tripura, and sikkim. that's eight states, dozens of distinct tribal and ethnic groups, and about as many genuinely different food traditions. they don't share a spice blend the way punjabi or hyderabadi cooking does. what they share is an approach. flavor comes from fermentation and smoking rather than a stacked masala, and the staples are rice and local greens rather than wheat and dairy. geography is a large part of why. the region connects to the rest of india only through the narrow siliguri corridor, sometimes called the "chicken's neck," while sharing long borders with tibet, myanmar, bhutan, and bangladesh. historically, trade and cultural exchange across those borders shaped the region's kitchens at least as much as anything arriving from delhi. fermentation as the region's spice rack where a punjabi or hyderabadi kitchen reaches for a garam masala blend, much of the northeast reaches for something fermented instead. bamboo shoot, fresh, dried, or fermented into a sour paste known as soibum in manipur or khorisa in assam, shows up across the region as a souring, funky base note. naga cooking in particular relies on akhuni (also spelled axone), fermented soybean with a pungency often compared to japanese natto, worked into pork and chicken dishes as the primary flavor driver rather than a background ingredient. bhut jolokia, the "ghost pepper" grown in assam and nagaland, held the guinness world record for hottest chili in the world from 2007 to 2011, and the indian army has tested it in smoke grenades. smoke, not cream, as the flavor base the region's meat cooking, especially pork, leans heavily on open-fire smoking rather than the dairy-rich gravies common further west and north; there's comparatively little use of cream, ghee, or yogurt as a curry base. assamese cooking adds its own signatures on top of this. masor tenga is a light, sour fish curry soured with tomato or lemon rather than tamarind. khar is built on an alkaline water filtered through banana-peel ash, a flavor and technique with no real parallel elsewhere in indian cooking. quick facts region eight northeastern states staple grain rice defining technique fermentation and smoking, not dairy-based gravies key historical moment geographic isolation via the siliguri corridor; closer historical trade ties to tibet and southeast asia than to mainland india signature dish smoked pork with bamboo shoot (naga) naga-style smoked pork ribs with bamboo shoot, a signature combination across nagaland. momos: a tibetan import that became a northeast and himalayan-india staple. signature dishes axone pork (nagaland): pork cooked with fermented soybean, one of the region's most distinctive flavor combinations. recipe → masor tenga (assam): a light, sour fish curry soured with tomato or lemon. recipe → khar (assam): a savory dish built on alkaline water filtered through banana-peel ash. recipe → bamboo shoot pickle : fermented or fresh bamboo shoot, used across nearly every state in the region. momos and thukpa (sikkim, arunachal pradesh): tibetan-influenced dumplings and noodle soup, staples in the himalayan-border states. recipe → recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian meal.

entries.title: Odia Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Odia (Odisha) cuisine: rice and pakhala, the giant temple kitchen at Puri, and the rasgulla that Odisha and Bengal both claim.
entries.text: odia cuisine odia cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of odia (odisha) cuisine: rice and pakhala, the giant temple kitchen at puri, and the rasgulla that odisha and bengal both claim. odia cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana east india odia cuisine a rice, mustard, and temple cuisine on the bay of bengal, lighter and less oily than its better-known neighbor. rice, the coast, and a lot of restraint odisha sits on the bay of bengal, between bengal to the northeast and the telugu south. its food shares plenty with bengali cooking: rice as the staple, mustard, freshwater fish, and a serious sweet tradition. but it pulls back on all of them. odia cooking is usually lighter, less oily, and more gently spiced than the food on either side of it. the everyday tempering is pancha phutana , a five-spice mix of mustard, cumin, fennel, fenugreek, and nigella seeds. the dish that sums up the cuisine is pakhala. in the heat of an odia summer, a common lunch is rice left to ferment overnight in water, served cool with salt, a little yogurt, and fried or mashed vegetables on the side. it cools the body and uses up the previous day's rice. odisha even marks a pakhala dibasa (pakhala day) every 20 march. the kitchen at the jagannath temple the biggest influence on odia food is the temple, not a royal court. at the jagannath temple in puri, the kitchen (the rosaghara) is one of the largest in the world and cooks for thousands of pilgrims a day. food is made in earthen pots stacked several high over wood fires, and by tradition the pot on top cooks first. what is offered to the deity is the mahaprasada, dozens of dishes known together as the chhappan bhoga, or "fifty-six offerings." it is all vegetarian and cooked without onion, garlic, tomato, or chili. once offered, it is sold and eaten side by side by pilgrims of every background at the ananda bazaar next to the temple. that plain, satvik, rice-and-dal cooking shaped a lot of odia home food too. in odisha the defining kitchen isn't a court or a restaurant. it's a temple that has cooked for pilgrims the same way for centuries. who really invented the rasgulla? odisha and bengal have argued for years over who created the rasgulla (rasagola). odisha's version, the pahala rasagola, is tied to the jagannath temple, where a chhena sweet has long been offered to the deities. bengal traces its rosogolla to the kolkata confectioner nobin chandra das in the 1860s. the dispute reached india's geographical indication (gi) system. odisha won a gi tag for "odisha rasagola" in 2019, two years after west bengal secured one for "banglar rosogolla." the tags recognize two regional versions rather than settling who was first. odisha's other signature sweet is chhena poda, or "burnt cheese," a baked block of fresh chhena and sugar with a caramelized crust, usually traced to the town of nayagarh. a coastline of its own along the coast, sea fish and prawns do the work that river fish does inland. dishes like chungudi malai, prawns in a mild coconut-milk gravy, point to odisha's long shoreline and its old sea trade with southeast asia. the state still marks that seafaring past every year at bali jatra, a festival in cuttack that remembers ancient voyages to bali and beyond. quick facts region odisha (formerly orissa), east coast staple grain rice defining technique earthen-pot temple cooking; pancha phutana five-spice; mustard and chhena sweets key site the jagannath temple kitchen at puri signature protein freshwater and sea fish, prawns chhena poda: a baked block of fresh chhena and sugar with a caramelized crust. pakhala: rice fermented overnight in water, served cool through the odia summer. signature dishes dalma : lentils cooked with vegetables and tempered with pancha phutana, a temple and everyday staple. recipe → pakhala : rice soaked or fermented in water, eaten cool with simple sides. recipe → macha besara : fish in a mustard-and-garlic gravy. recipe → chungudi malai : prawns in a mild coconut-milk curry. recipe → santula : a light, gently spiced mix of steamed vegetables. recipe → chhena poda : baked "burnt cheese" sweet with a caramelized crust. recipe → rasagola (pahala) : chhena balls in syrup, the temple-linked odia version. recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian meal.

entries.title: Parsi Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Parsi cuisine: the Zoroastrian migration from Persia to Gujarat, dhansak and the fourth day, eggs on everything, the Irani cafes of Bombay, and the wedding feast.
entries.text: parsi cuisine parsi cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of parsi cuisine: the zoroastrian migration from persia to gujarat, dhansak and the fourth day, eggs on everything, the irani cafes of bombay, and the wedding feast. parsi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana a community, not a region parsi cuisine persian technique carried into gujarat by refugees and rebuilt on indian ingredients, into a kitchen that is sweet, sour and hot in the same mouthful. milk and sugar: a cuisine that arrived by boat parsi food has no zone on this site's map, and that is the point. every other cuisine here belongs to a territory; parsi cooking belongs to a community. the parsis are zoroastrians who left persia after the arab conquest of the seventh century and reached the gujarat coast in waves between roughly the eighth and tenth centuries, landing at sanjan in valsad district. they came as refugees with a religion, a calendar and a set of kitchen habits, and no land of their own. what they built afterwards was a food culture attached to families, fire temples and neighbourhoods rather than to a stretch of soil. the community's founding story is a story about food. the qissa-i sanjan, a persian narrative poem written down in 1599, records that the local ruler jadi rana sent the new arrivals a vessel of milk filled to the brim, meaning his kingdom was full. their priest stirred in sugar and returned it, meaning they would dissolve into it and sweeten it without displacing anyone. he was granted asylum on conditions: adopt the local language, dress the women in the sari, marry by local custom, and carry no weapons. gujarati became the household tongue, and the kitchen followed the same bargain — persian instincts, gujarati groceries. sweet, sour and hot in the same mouthful persian cooking gave the parsis dried fruit and nuts in savoury dishes, rice cooked as a centrepiece rather than a filler, meat braised slowly with onion, and a taste for sourness from pomegranate and vinegar. gujarat supplied jaggery, tamarind, coconut, curry leaves, kokum and the local habit of putting sugar into things that other kitchens keep savoury. the two did not sit side by side; they merged. the result is a palate that runs sweet, sour and hot at once, which is unusual in india — most regional cuisines pick two of the three. the engine of the kitchen is a masala of onion browned patiently to a deep colour, garlic, ginger, cumin and chilli, sharpened at the end with vinegar, tamarind or lime and rounded with jaggery. it appears in the patio, the sweet-sour-hot pickle-curry that is the family's default treatment for prawns and fish. it appears in dhansak. when the parsis moved south to bombay in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and prospered under the east india company as shipbuilders, brokers and traders, the kitchen picked up a further british layer: custards, puddings, cutlets, oxtail stew and a fondness for worcestershire sauce. milk filled to the brim, sugar stirred in and returned. a thousand years later the kitchen still works that way — nothing displaced, everything sweetened. dhansak, and the fourth day dhansak is the dish most outsiders name first, and the one most often served wrongly. it is mutton on the bone simmered with three or more lentils and a mass of vegetables — pumpkin, brinjal, fenugreek leaves — until the whole thing is puréed to a thick, dark, sour-hot gravy, seasoned with a dhansak masala of its own and finished with tamarind. it is eaten with caramelised brown rice, kachumber and fried papad, and it is sunday lunch in most parsi households, followed by an afternoon nobody expects to be productive. it is also funerary food. zoroastrian custom holds that the soul lingers for four days after death, and the family observes restrictions during that period, including abstaining from meat. on the fourth day, after the prayers, the household returns to normal eating with dhansak. because of that association it is not cooked on birthdays, weddings, navjotes or auspicious days — a parsi host serving dhansak at a wedding would be making a genuine mistake. festive occasions call for pulao instead. eggs on everything, and the irani cafe the parsi kitchen treats the egg as a technique rather than a dish. almost anything can be spread in a pan, levelled, and finished with eggs broken over the top: potatoes for papeta par eeda, tomatoes for tamota par eeda, okra, bananas, fried potato straws, even leftovers. akuri is the other direction — eggs scrambled soft and wet with onion, tomato, coriander, green chilli and ginger, never allowed to set dry, and eaten with pao at any hour. the joke that parsis put eggs on everything is not really a joke. that habit reached the general public through the irani cafes of bombay, opened from the late nineteenth century by zoroastrian immigrants from iran — a later, separate migration from the parsis, though the food overlapped. bentwood chairs, marble-topped tables, mirrors, lists of house rules, bun maska, irani chai, mutton samosas, kheema pao and akuri. britannia, kyani, yazdani and ideal fed clerks and students without asking anyone's caste, which in the bombay of the period was itself the attraction. fewer than a couple of dozen survive, and their decline is watched closely, because for most indians the cafe is the only parsi kitchen they have ever eaten in. the wedding feast a parsi wedding dinner is served on banana leaves in a set order, and the order barely varies. it opens with rotli and a sweet — often the fudge-like ravo — then patra ni machhi, pomfret smeared with a green coconut-coriander-chilli chutney, wrapped in banana leaf and steamed until the leaf perfumes the fish. then sali boti, mutton in a sweet-sour gravy heaped with matchstick potato straws, or its chicken cousin salli marghi. then a pulao-dal, usually with berry pulao alongside: rice with mutton and the sour dried barberries brought from iran, a dish popularised in bombay by the britannia cafe. dessert is lagan nu custard, the wedding custard — milk reduced slowly, enriched with eggs, nutmeg and cardamom, scattered with almonds and pistachios, and baked until the top browns. the whole meal is cooked by hereditary

entries.title: Punjabi Cuisine
entries.snippet: How the tandoor and Punjab's wheat belt shaped its cuisine, and how Partition-era refugees invented butter chicken in Delhi.
entries.text: punjabi cuisine punjabi cuisine: history & iconic dishes how the tandoor and punjab's wheat belt shaped its cuisine, and how partition-era refugees invented butter chicken in delhi. punjabi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana north india punjabi cuisine tandoors, wheat, and dairy, plus the refugee kitchens of 1947 that turned punjabi food into india's most recognized export. the land of five rivers punjab takes its name from panj āb (five rivers), and that geography built the cuisine long before any dynasty or border did. the indus plain is some of the most fertile farmland in south asia, and for centuries it has produced wheat rather than rice as its staple grain, along with the dairy that comes naturally with extensive cattle and buffalo farming. roti, paratha, naan, ghee, makkhan (butter), lassi, paneer. the core of punjabi cooking is really the core of punjabi agriculture. the tandoor, the clay oven now inseparable from punjabi food, isn't originally punjabi at all. it arrived with central asian and mughal influence, likely by the 16th century. what punjab did was make it central. tandoori roti, naan, and tandoor-roasted meats became the backbone of a cooking style built around live fire and dairy-based marinades. 1947, and the invention of "indian restaurant food" the single biggest turning point in punjabi cuisine's history isn't ancient. it's 1947. partition displaced millions of punjabis from what became west punjab, pakistan, and a large number resettled in delhi. among them were restaurateurs who rebuilt their trade from scratch, and it's this generation that is widely credited with inventing what most of the world now thinks of as "indian food." butter chicken is the clearest example. the story, credited to kundan lal gujral of delhi's moti mahal restaurant, is that leftover tandoori chicken was simmered in a tomato-butter gravy to keep it from drying out. that practical fix became a signature dish. dal makhani, black lentils finished the same way with butter and cream, followed the same logic. both dishes are, in culinary-history terms, remarkably recent. they're refugee-kitchen inventions from the late 1940s that went on to define an entire cuisine's global reputation. roti and dairy built the everyday punjabi table. a generation of refugee restaurateurs in 1940s delhi built the version the rest of the world knows. village food vs. restaurant food it's worth separating the two punjabi cuisines that coexist today. one is the everyday rural table. sarson da saag (mustard greens, slow-cooked with spices) eaten with makki di roti (cornmeal flatbread), along with simple dals, buttermilk, and pickles, food built for farming families and cold punjab winters. the other is the richer, dairy-heavy restaurant repertoire of butter chicken, dal makhani, and paneer dishes, built for the diaspora and now exported worldwide. both are authentically punjabi. they just come from different centuries and different kitchens. quick facts region north india (punjab, extending into delhi & the diaspora) staple grain wheat defining technique tandoor (clay oven) cooking key historical moment partition, 1947: refugee restaurateurs in delhi signature fat ghee & butter butter chicken: invented at delhi's moti mahal in the late 1940s. chole bhature: spiced chickpeas with deep-fried leavened bread. signature dishes butter chicken : tandoori chicken simmered in a tomato, butter, and cream gravy. recipe → dal makhani : black lentils and kidney beans, slow-cooked with butter and cream. recipe → sarson da saag & makki di roti : mustard greens with cornmeal flatbread, a winter staple. recipe → chole bhature : spiced chickpea curry with fried bread, a delhi-punjabi street food classic. recipe → amritsari kulcha : stuffed leavened flatbread from amritsar, baked in a tandoor. lassi : a churned yogurt drink, sweet or salted. recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian meal.

entries.title: Rajasthani Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Rajasthani cuisine: desert cooking, Rajput royal kitchens, and the Marwari vegetarian tradition.
entries.text: rajasthani cuisine rajasthani cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of rajasthani cuisine: desert cooking, rajput royal kitchens, and the marwari vegetarian tradition. rajasthani cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana northwest india rajasthani cuisine cooking adapted to the desert, built around scarce water and ingredients that keep. two very different food traditions grew up inside it. cooking for the thar desert much of rajasthan sits within or on the edge of the thar desert, and the cuisine answers to that environment more directly than almost any other indian regional tradition. fresh vegetables were historically scarce and water was precious. so the cooking developed around ingredients that could survive drought and long storage. these were dried lentils and beans, dried desert berries and pods such as ker and sangri (gathered from native desert shrubs), buttermilk and other dairy standing in for fresh produce, and plenty of ghee to add richness where fresh ingredients couldn't. two traditions, one region rajasthan's food history carries a real internal split. on one side is the rajput tradition, the warrior-noble class whose royal kitchens grew out of hunting culture and historically included game and meat. laal maas ("red meat"), a fiery mutton curry tied to royal rajput feasts, is the clearest surviving example. on the other side is the marwari tradition, rajasthan's major merchant community, historically jain or vaishnav hindu, and strictly vegetarian. the marwari community's trading networks reached across india, and they carried rajasthani vegetarian food far beyond the state's borders, including what's now sold across the country as "rajasthani thali." a royal hunting curry and a merchant caste's strict vegetarianism grew up in the same desert, and both are equally "rajasthani." dal baati churma: a meal engineered for storage the state's signature dish shows how the whole cuisine works. baati are hard wheat-flour rolls, traditionally baked (originally in embers) until dense and dry. it's a bread built to last rather than to be eaten fresh and soft. they're served crushed into ghee alongside dal (lentils) and churma (a sweet, crumbled wheat-and-jaggery mixture). every part of the dish is built for a hot, dry climate and for keeping without refrigeration, and that idea runs through nearly the whole cuisine. quick facts region northwest india (rajasthan, including the thar desert) staple grain wheat, millet (bajra) defining technique preservation-first cooking: dried lentils, dairy, minimal fresh water/vegetables key historical split rajput (royal, meat-eating) vs. marwari (merchant, strictly vegetarian) signature fat ghee a rajasthani thali: the marwari vegetarian tradition, carried nationwide by the merchant diaspora. kachori: a deep-fried, spiced-lentil-stuffed pastry. signature dishes dal baati churma : hard wheat rolls with lentils and a sweet crumbled wheat dish. recipe → laal maas : a fiery, red-chili mutton curry from the rajput royal tradition. recipe → gatte ki sabzi : gram-flour dumplings in a spiced yogurt gravy, a classic "no fresh vegetables needed" dish. recipe → ker sangri : a dish of dried desert berries and beans, unique to the region. recipe → kachori : a deep-fried pastry stuffed with spiced lentils or onions. recipe → recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian meal.

entries.title: Sindhi Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of Sindhi cuisine: a riverine, Sufi and mercantile kitchen from Sindh in present-day Pakistan, carried into India after 1947 by a community without a territory — sai bhaji, koki, dal pakwan and Sindhi kadhi.
entries.text: sindhi cuisine sindhi cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of sindhi cuisine: a riverine, sufi and mercantile kitchen from sindh in present-day pakistan, carried into india after 1947 by a community without a territory — sai bhaji, koki, dal pakwan and sindhi kadhi. sindhi cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana a cuisine carried across a border sindhi cuisine the kitchen of a river province in present-day pakistan, kept alive in india by the community that left it — sour, onion-heavy, and cooked without a homeland for close to eighty years. a river, a shrine and a trading house sindh is the lower indus: a strip of irrigated land running down to the arabian sea, with desert on one side and the delta on the other. everything about the old sindhi plate follows from that geography. rice grew along the canals and wheat behind them; lotus stem — bhee — was pulled out of the standing water of the ponds and became one of the few vegetables a cuisine anywhere treats as a staple; freshwater palla fish ran up the indus in season and was cooked over a slow fire on one side only. the province was also a corridor rather than a cul-de-sac, sitting on the sea route to the gulf and the land route to kandahar, and dried fruit, sour agents and whole spices came in along both. two social facts shaped it further. sindh was sufi country, its shrines at sehwan and bhit shah drawing hindus and muslims to the same courtyards, and the food of the two communities diverged far less than it did elsewhere in the subcontinent — the same kadhi, the same koki, the same habit of browning onion until it collapses. and the sindhi hindus were overwhelmingly a mercantile caste group, shopkeepers, moneylenders and traders rather than farmers. their cooking is trader's cooking: fast on a working morning, generous on a sunday, and built around things that keep. 1947, and a cuisine that outlived its territory partition cut sindh away whole. the province went to pakistan intact — it was not divided the way punjab and bengal were — and the sindhi hindu minority, perhaps a million people, left over the following two years by ship from karachi and by train through rajasthan. they did not arrive anywhere in a block. they settled in bombay, in gujarat at gandhidham and adipur, in ajmer, in jaipur, in delhi, and above all in the emptied military camp outside bombay that they renamed ulhasnagar, where barracks became lanes of shops. sindhi is the only major cuisine on this site whose home region lies outside india, and the map of india's cuisine zones has no sindhi zone to give it. it is carried by a community, not by a territory. what is striking is how little the food dissolved. deprived of sindh's lotus ponds and its palla, the cuisine kept its logic and substituted where it had to: bhee travelled in from kashmir and bengal to city markets, and the fish quietly dropped out. the sunday kadhi, the cheti chand sweets marking the sindhi new year, the koki packed for a train — these survived because they were domestic rather than public. there is barely any sindhi restaurant tradition to speak of, and for decades almost no sindhi cookbooks; the recipes moved from mother to daughter across three cities at once. that is also why the dishes are so consistent from one household to another and so nearly invisible on a national menu. sindh went to pakistan whole, and the cuisine came to india in the hands of the people who left. it is held by a community, not a place on the map. the everyday plate the weekday centre of it is sai bhaji: spinach cooked right down with chana dal and whatever else is in the house — dill, sorrel, aubergine, carrot, tomato — into a soft green mash, eaten with plain rice. it is one dish doing the work of three, vegetable and dal and gravy together, and it is the thing most sindhis mean when they say they want home food. alongside it sits koki, a thick crumbly flatbread kneaded with chopped onion, coriander and green chilli, half-cooked on the tawa, taken off, pressed thicker and returned to finish. it stays edible for two days, which is exactly why a trading family made it, and it is still the bread that goes into a lunchbox. the weekend is more formal. sunday lunch is sindhi kadhi — a roasted gram flour and tamarind curry, nothing like the yogurt kadhis of gujarat or punjab, loaded with drumstick, okra, potato and cluster beans — poured over bhuga chawal, rice browned in caramelised onion. sunday breakfast is dal pakwan: soft chana dal under chaat masala and raw onion, with crisp fried maida discs broken over it, sweet with tamarind chutney on the side. it is the one sindhi dish that has genuinely escaped the community, sold now off carts in mumbai and pune to people who have no idea where it came from. sour, hot, and built on onion the palate is the giveaway. sindhi cooking is sourer than anything around it and reaches for tamarind first, then dried pomegranate seed — anardana — and amchur, often two of them in the same pot. that sourness runs against a real chilli heat and a heavy hand with garam masala, and the result is sharp rather than rich. sindhi biryani is the extreme case: mutton, potato, yogurt and dried plums layered with far more chilli and far more sour than a hyderabadi or lucknowi cook would allow, and it is the version of biryani that pakistan now eats as a national dish, on both sides of a border the recipe ignores. underneath all of it is onion, used in quantities that mark the cuisine out. it is browned to a dark collapse for bhugal, the base of half the meat dishes; it is smothered raw with the main ingredient and a wet masala in the seyal method that gives seyal bhaji and seyal gosht their name; it goes uncooked into koki dough and raw over dal pakwan. garlic follows it closely. there is no restraint being exercised here and none was intended — this is a cuisine of strong flavours from a place that traded in them, still being cooked, several generations later, several hundred miles from home. quick facts region sindh, on the lower indus in present-day pakistan; cooked in india by the post-1947 sindhi community in mumbai, ulhasnagar, gujarat and rajasthan staple grain rice, with wheat and pearl millet for the breads defining technique bhugal, onion browne

entries.title: Tamil Nadu Cuisine
entries.snippet: The history of South Indian cuisine: rice, fermentation, and how chili peppers from the Americas transformed Andhra cooking.
entries.text: tamil nadu cuisine tamil nadu cuisine: history & iconic dishes the history of south indian cuisine: rice, fermentation, and how chili peppers from the americas transformed andhra cooking. tamil nadu cuisine: history & iconic dishes | khaana south india tamil nadu cuisine rice, lentils, and fermentation. four distinct food traditions built on the same ancient staples. four cuisines, one umbrella term "south indian food" is a handy shorthand, but it flattens four genuinely distinct traditions: tamil, kerala (malayali), karnataka (kannadiga), and andhra/telangana (telugu). they share a common base of rice as the staple grain, lentils for protein, and a reliance on fermentation and tempering (tadka, or whole spices bloomed in hot oil). but they diverge sharply in heat, fat, and flavor. kerala leans on coconut oil and coconut milk. andhra is famous even within india for being the spiciest of the major regional cuisines. tamil nadu's chettinad region built its own tradition around dry-roasted whole spices. an old fermentation tradition the dosa and idli are now the most globally recognized south indian foods, and both rest on an old technique. you soak and grind rice and urad dal (black gram), then let the batter ferment overnight before cooking. the fermentation develops flavor and also makes the batter's nutrients easier to digest. references to dosa-like foods appear in tamil and kannada literature going back over a thousand years. that makes it one of the older cooking techniques still in continuous use on the subcontinent, well before chilies, tomatoes, or potatoes arrived. rice, lentils, and fermentation are the old core. chili heat, now andhra's calling card, is a 16th-century import. the chili pepper's arrival chili peppers are not native to india at all, one of the most-quoted facts of indian food history. they arrived via portuguese trade routes after 1498, part of the broader "columbian exchange" that moved new world crops into asia. before then, heat in south indian cooking came from black pepper (a native kerala export that drove centuries of spice-trade interest from rome to europe) and from ginger. chilies caught on fast, nowhere more than in andhra pradesh, whose cuisine is now defined by a level of heat that postdates the mughal empire itself. coffee, coconuts, and the meal as a system the south indian thali (or "meals," as it's often called in tamil nadu and karnataka) follows a plan. rice is the anchor, with sambar, rasam, kootu, and chutneys eaten in a set order, usually finishing with yogurt rice to cool the palate. it's typically served on a banana leaf. filter coffee, brewed with a metal filter and served with frothed milk, became a south indian institution in the 19th and 20th centuries. it remains as culturally central as the dosa itself. quick facts region tamil nadu, kerala, karnataka, andhra pradesh & telangana staple grain rice defining technique batter fermentation & oil tempering (tadka) key historical moment post-1498 arrival of the chili pepper via portuguese trade signature fat coconut oil (kerala/coastal tn), sesame & groundnut oil elsewhere idli and sambar: steamed fermented rice cakes with a tamarind lentil stew. sambar: a tamarind-based lentil stew that anchors the south indian thali. signature dishes dosa : a fermented rice-and-lentil crepe, often filled with spiced potato (masala dosa). recipe → idli : steamed fermented rice cakes, typically eaten with sambar and chutney. recipe → sambar : a tamarind-based lentil and vegetable stew. recipe → rasam : a thin, peppery tamarind soup, often served after sambar. recipe → uttapam : a thicker, savory pancake made from the same fermented batter as dosa. recipe → filter coffee : south india's defining beverage tradition. recipes based on ingredients → tell us what is in your kitchen, and khaana will help you cook an authentic indian meal.

entries.title: Andhra Kodi Kura
entries.snippet: bone-in chicken curry, fiercely red and thick with browned onion
entries.text: andhra kodi kura andhra bone-in chicken curry, fiercely red and thick with browned onion gluten-free dairy-free nut-free healthier chicken onion tomato ginger garlic green chilli red chilli powder coriander powder turmeric powder black pepper garam masala cloves cinnamon bay leaf poppy seeds (khus khus) curry leaves groundnut oil coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water heat the oil in a kadhai until it shimmers, add the cloves, cinnamon and bay leaf and let them swell for 30 seconds. add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and fry over medium heat for 14 to 16 minutes, until deep brown at the edges and shrunk to a third of the volume. stir in the ginger-garlic paste, green chillies and curry leaves and cook 3 minutes until the raw garlic smell has gone completely. add the tomato and cook 6 minutes, pressing it against the pan, until it breaks down and the mixture pulls together. add the chilli powder, coriander powder, remaining turmeric and crushed pepper and fry 2 minutes over low heat with a splash of water so the spices do not catch. tip in the marinated chicken and turn it in the masala over high heat for 8 minutes, until every piece is coated and the edges have seized and browned. stir in the poppy seed paste and the salt, then pour in 400ml water and bring to a boil. lower the heat, cover, and simmer 20 minutes, until the chicken is tender and a thigh piece comes off the bone easily. uncover and cook 8 minutes more on medium heat, until the gravy clings to the chicken and a slick of red oil rises to the top. sprinkle over the garam masala and coriander leaves, cover, and rest 5 minutes off the heat.

entries.title: Bobbatlu
entries.snippet: thin griddled flatbreads stuffed with sweet chana dal and jaggery
entries.text: bobbatlu andhra thin griddled flatbreads stuffed with sweet chana dal and jaggery vegetarian nut-free chana dal jaggery plain flour (maida) atta (wholewheat flour) turmeric powder green cardamom nutmeg ghee salt water knead the maida, atta, salt, turmeric and about 120ml water into a very soft, sticky dough — softer than chapati dough, almost batter-like at the edges. pour 4 tbsp of the melted ghee over the dough, cover, and leave it 3 hours at room temperature. it should be slack and silky when you come back. pressure cook the drained chana dal with 400ml water for 4 whistles, until a grain crushes to paste between two fingers. drain the dal thoroughly, then blitz or mash it to a smooth paste. cook the dal paste with the jaggery in a heavy pan over medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring constantly, until it thickens and comes away from the sides in a single mass. stir in the cardamom and nutmeg, spread the filling on a plate and cool it completely, then roll it into 8 equal balls. oil your palms, take a lump of dough the size of a lime, flatten it on a greased sheet of banana leaf or baking paper, place a filling ball in the centre and gather the dough over it. with greased fingertips, pat the parcel out to a thin 15cm round — do not use a rolling pin, it will tear. heat a tawa over medium heat and flip the bobbattu onto it, paper side up, then peel the paper away. cook 60 to 90 seconds a side, brushing with ghee, until brown spots appear and the surface puffs in patches. slide it onto a plate, brush with more ghee, and repeat with the rest.

entries.title: Chepala Pulusu
entries.snippet: fish simmered in a dark tamarind gravy sharpened with fenugreek
entries.text: chepala pulusu andhra fish simmered in a dark tamarind gravy sharpened with fenugreek pescatarian gluten-free dairy-free nut-free healthier fish (firm fillets or steaks) tamarind onion tomato garlic ginger green chilli red chilli powder coriander powder turmeric powder fenugreek seeds (methi) mustard seeds cumin seeds dried red chillies curry leaves rice flour jaggery sesame oil (gingelly / til) coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water heat the sesame oil in a wide kadhai and crackle the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, dried red chillies and curry leaves. add the onion and cook 10 minutes over medium heat until soft and golden brown. stir in the garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry 2 minutes until fragrant. add the tomato and cook 6 minutes until it collapses completely. add the chilli powder, coriander powder and remaining turmeric with 2 tbsp water and fry 2 minutes until the paste darkens to brick red. pour in the tamarind pulp and 500ml water, add the salt and jaggery, and boil hard for 12 minutes to cook off the raw tamarind edge. stir in the rice flour slurry and cook 2 minutes until the gravy thickens enough to coat a spoon. slide the fish steaks in in a single layer, spoon gravy over them, and simmer uncovered on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes. sprinkle over the fenugreek powder, shake the pan once, and take it off the heat. scatter the coriander leaves and leave it to stand at least 2 hours before serving.

entries.title: Dosakaya Pappu
entries.snippet: everyday toor dal cooked down with yellow cucumber and tamarind
entries.text: dosakaya pappu andhra everyday toor dal cooked down with yellow cucumber and tamarind vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free nut-free healthier toor dal (pigeon pea) cucumber tomato green chilli onion garlic tamarind turmeric powder red chilli powder mustard seeds cumin seeds dried red chillies curry leaves asafoetida (hing) groundnut oil coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water pressure cook the dal with the cucumber, tomato, green chillies, turmeric and 600ml water for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop naturally. open the cooker and mash the dal lightly against the side with the back of a ladle, leaving some cucumber cubes whole. stir in the tamarind pulp, chilli powder, salt and the remaining 100ml water, and simmer uncovered for 8 minutes. meanwhile heat the oil in a small pan and crackle the mustard seeds until they pop, about 30 seconds. add the cumin, dried red chillies, garlic and curry leaves and fry 1 minute until the garlic is golden and the leaves go crisp. take the pan off the heat, stir in the asafoetida, and let it sizzle for 5 seconds. pour the tempering into the dal, add the raw onion if using, and simmer 2 minutes more. finish with the coriander leaves and check the salt — it should taste sour, then hot, then savoury.

entries.title: Gongura Pachadi
entries.snippet: fierce sour-leaf chutney, eaten by the spoonful with hot rice
entries.text: gongura pachadi andhra fierce sour-leaf chutney, eaten by the spoonful with hot rice vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free nut-free amaranth greens (chaulai) tamarind dried red chillies green chilli garlic sesame oil (gingelly / til) mustard seeds cumin seeds fenugreek seeds (methi) turmeric powder asafoetida (hing) curry leaves salt heat 2 tbsp of the sesame oil in a kadhai and fry the dried red chillies, fenugreek seeds and half the cumin over low heat for 2 minutes, until the chillies darken by a shade and smell toasty. lift the spices out onto a plate and set them aside to cool completely. in the same pan add another 2 tbsp oil and the garlic, and fry 2 minutes until the cloves are pale gold at the edges. add the greens a large handful at a time with the green chillies and turmeric, and cook over medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the leaves collapse and the pan goes almost dry. stir in the tamarind pulp and salt and cook another 4 minutes, until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan in a single mass. cool the greens fully, then grind them with the toasted spices to a coarse paste — no water at all, and it should still have some texture. heat the last tbsp of oil, crackle the mustard seeds and remaining cumin, add the curry leaves and asafoetida, and pour the whole tempering over the chutney. fold the tempering through and taste for salt and sourness — it should hit sour first, then heat.

entries.title: Gutti Vankaya Kura
entries.snippet: small eggplants stuffed with a peanut, sesame and coconut masala in tamarind gravy
entries.text: gutti vankaya kura andhra small eggplants stuffed with a peanut, sesame and coconut masala in tamarind gravy vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free healthier eggplant / brinjal peanuts sesame seeds dried coconut (copra) coriander powder cumin seeds red chilli powder turmeric powder onion garlic ginger tamarind jaggery groundnut oil mustard seeds curry leaves coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water dry-roast the peanuts over medium heat for 4 minutes until blistered, then the sesame for 1 minute until they jump, then the coconut for 1 minute until sandy gold. grind the cooled peanuts, sesame and coconut with the coriander powder, cumin, chilli powder, turmeric and 1 tsp salt to a coarse, dryish powder. drain the eggplants, pat them dry, and press about a tablespoon of the masala into each one, prising the quarters apart with your thumb. keep the leftover masala. heat 4 tbsp of the oil in a wide kadhai, lay the stuffed eggplants in a single layer and fry them 6 to 8 minutes, turning gently, until the skins blister and go glossy. lift them out. add the remaining oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the curry leaves, onion, garlic and ginger and cook 8 minutes until the onion is soft and lightly browned. stir in the leftover masala powder and fry it for 3 minutes, until it darkens and smells nutty rather than raw. pour in the tamarind pulp and 300ml water, add the jaggery and remaining salt, and bring to a simmer. slide the eggplants back in, spoon gravy over them, cover and cook on low heat for 15 to 18 minutes, until a knife slips into an eggplant with no resistance. uncover and simmer 5 minutes more until the gravy thickens and oil beads on the surface. scatter the coriander leaves over and rest it 10 minutes off the heat before serving with rice.

entries.title: Pulihora
entries.snippet: sour, peppery tamarind rice, the temple food of the telugu country
entries.text: pulihora andhra sour, peppery tamarind rice, the temple food of the telugu country vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free healthier rice (short/medium grain) tamarind sesame oil (gingelly / til) peanuts chana dal urad dal (black gram) mustard seeds fenugreek seeds (methi) sesame seeds dried red chillies green chilli turmeric powder asafoetida (hing) curry leaves jaggery salt water spread the cooked rice on a large tray, drizzle over 2 tbsp of the sesame oil and 1/2 tsp turmeric, and fork it through gently. heat the remaining 4 tbsp oil in a kadhai over medium heat and fry the peanuts for 3 minutes until they turn a shade darker and smell roasted, then scoop them out. into the same oil add the chana dal and urad dal and fry 2 minutes until both are reddish-gold and crisp — they are the crunch in the finished rice. add the mustard seeds and let them pop, about 30 seconds, then the dried red chillies, green chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida. pour in the tamarind pulp with the rest of the turmeric and the salt, and bring it to a hard simmer. cook the tamarind mixture for 10 to 12 minutes, until it thickens, darkens and the oil separates and pools at the edges of the pan. stir in the jaggery and the powdered fenugreek, cook 1 minute more, then take the pan off the heat. pour two-thirds of the tamarind paste over the rice and fold it in with a flat spoon, lifting rather than stirring, until every grain is pale gold. scatter over the fried peanuts and the sesame powder, fold once more, and taste — add the rest of the paste if you want it sharper. cover and leave it 30 minutes before serving so the rice absorbs the dressing evenly.

entries.title: Punugulu
entries.snippet: crisp fermented-batter fritters, the roadside snack of the coast
entries.text: punugulu andhra crisp fermented-batter fritters, the roadside snack of the coast vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free nut-free healthier rice (short/medium grain) urad dal (black gram) rava / sooji (semolina) rice flour onion green chilli ginger cumin seeds curry leaves coriander leaves (cilantro) baking soda neutral oil salt water stir the rice flour and rava into the fermented batter and let it sit 15 minutes to hydrate. fold in the onion, green chillies, ginger, cumin, curry leaves, coriander leaves and salt. check the consistency: it should drop off a spoon in a thick lump, not a ribbon. add the baking soda only if the batter tastes flat. heat the oil in a kadhai to 170c — a drop of batter should sink briefly and rise within 3 seconds, fizzing. drop in walnut-sized spoonfuls of batter, 8 or 10 at a time, keeping the pan uncrowded. fry 4 to 5 minutes, turning them once they float, until deep golden brown all over and audibly crisp when tapped with the spoon. lift them out onto a rack, not paper — paper traps steam and softens the bottoms. let the oil come back up to temperature for a minute before the next batch, and serve hot with coconut or peanut chutney.

entries.title: Royyala Iguru
entries.snippet: prawns cooked dry in a thick masala until it clings to every one
entries.text: royyala iguru andhra prawns cooked dry in a thick masala until it clings to every one pescatarian gluten-free dairy-free nut-free healthier prawns onion tomato ginger garlic green chilli red chilli powder coriander powder turmeric powder black pepper garam masala curry leaves groundnut oil lemon / lime coriander leaves (cilantro) salt heat the oil in a kadhai over medium-high heat and fry the onion for 10 minutes, until soft and browning at the edges. add the garlic, ginger, green chillies and curry leaves and cook 2 minutes until the garlic loses its raw edge. add the tomato and cook 8 minutes, mashing it down, until it is completely broken and the oil starts to show at the sides. stir in the chilli powder, coriander powder, remaining turmeric and crushed pepper and fry 2 minutes on low heat. add the salt and cook the masala another 3 minutes until it is thick enough to hold the mark of a spoon. raise the heat to high, tip in the dried prawns and stir them through the masala for 3 to 4 minutes, until they curl into loose cs and turn opaque coral. take the pan off the heat and sprinkle over the garam masala. squeeze in the lemon juice, scatter the coriander leaves and toss once.

entries.title: Ulavacharu
entries.snippet: the dark, smoky horse gram broth of the coast, sour and deeply savoury
entries.text: ulavacharu andhra the dark, smoky horse gram broth of the coast, sour and deeply savoury vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free nut-free healthier horse gram (kulith) tamarind onion garlic green chilli red chilli powder turmeric powder coriander powder jaggery mustard seeds cumin seeds fenugreek seeds (methi) dried red chillies curry leaves sesame oil (gingelly / til) coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water drain the soaked horse gram, rinse it, and pressure cook with 1.5 litres of fresh water and the turmeric for 8 whistles, then let the pressure fall on its own. strain the cooked gram over a bowl, keeping every drop of the dark cooking liquid — that liquid is the dish. crush about a quarter of the cooked grains to a paste and stir it back into the liquid to give the broth body. pour the broth into a heavy pan with the remaining 500ml water and bring it to a steady simmer. heat the sesame oil in a small pan, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, fenugreek, dried red chillies and curry leaves and fry 1 minute until fragrant. add the onion and garlic to the tempering and cook 6 minutes until soft and just golden, then tip the whole lot into the simmering broth. add the tamarind pulp, green chillies, chilli powder, coriander powder, jaggery and salt, and simmer uncovered. let it reduce for 45 to 60 minutes over low heat, stirring occasionally, until it darkens to the colour of strong coffee and coats the back of a spoon. taste and adjust — it should be sour and smoky first, with the heat arriving after. scatter the coriander leaves over and serve hot in bowls alongside plain rice.

entries.title: Ball Curry
entries.snippet: beef meatballs poached in a thin red coconut gravy, the Sunday lunch of Calcutta Anglo-Indian homes
entries.text: ball curry anglo-indian beef meatballs poached in a thin red coconut gravy, the sunday lunch of calcutta anglo-indian homes nut-free healthier beef sliced bread milk eggs onion ginger garlic green chilli coriander leaves (cilantro) black pepper red chilli powder turmeric powder coriander powder cumin powder (jeera) tomato coconut milk potato neutral oil water salt mix the mince with the squeezed bread, beaten egg, grated onion, half the ginger-garlic paste, the chopped green chilli, 2 tbsp coriander leaves, the black pepper and 1 tsp salt. roll into balls the size of a walnut, about 20 of them, and chill 20 minutes. heat the oil in a wide pan and cook the sliced onion until soft and gold, 10 to 12 minutes. add the remaining ginger-garlic paste and fry 2 minutes. add the chilli powder, turmeric, coriander and cumin powders with a splash of water and fry 2 minutes until the oil takes on colour. add the tomato and cook until it collapses and the oil separates at the edges, 7 to 8 minutes. pour in the water, add the potato and salt, and bring to a steady simmer for 10 minutes. lower the balls in one at a time. do not stir for the first 5 minutes; shake the pan instead. simmer uncovered 15 minutes, turning the balls gently once, until they are firm and cooked through. stir in the coconut milk and simmer very gently 5 more minutes. check the salt, scatter the remaining coriander leaves and serve with yellow coconut rice.

entries.title: Country Captain Chicken
entries.snippet: dry-fried chicken buried in browned onion and whole red chillies, barely any gravy
entries.text: country captain chicken anglo-indian dry-fried chicken buried in browned onion and whole red chillies, barely any gravy gluten-free dairy-free nut-free chicken onion dried red chillies black pepper turmeric powder ginger garlic green chilli curry leaves vinegar sugar neutral oil coriander leaves (cilantro) salt heat the oil in a wide kadhai and fry three-quarters of the sliced onion over medium heat until brown and crisp at the edges, 15 to 18 minutes. lift out and drain. in the same oil, fry the whole dried chillies and curry leaves for 20 seconds until the chillies darken and smell toasty. add the remaining raw onion and cook 5 minutes until soft and translucent. turn the heat high, add the marinated chicken and fry hard for 10 minutes, turning the pieces so every side takes colour. lower the heat, cover and cook 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once or twice. the chicken releases its own liquid and cooks in it. uncover, raise the heat and cook off the liquid until the pieces are coated and shining rather than sitting in sauce, about 5 minutes. crush most of the reserved fried onion between your fingers and stir it in with the remaining black pepper, the slit green chillies and the sugar. splash in the vinegar, toss for 1 minute and take the pan off the heat. scatter the rest of the fried onion and the coriander leaves over the top and serve with plain rice or bread.

entries.title: Kalkals
entries.snippet: little curls of coconut-milk dough deep-fried crisp and frosted with sugar, the Christmas sweet
entries.text: kalkals anglo-indian little curls of coconut-milk dough deep-fried crisp and frosted with sugar, the christmas sweet vegetarian plain flour (maida) rava / sooji (semolina) coconut milk eggs ghee sugar green cardamom neutral oil water salt rub the melted ghee into the maida, rava, 3 tbsp sugar, cardamom and salt with your fingertips until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs. work in the beaten egg, then add the coconut milk a little at a time until you have a firm, smooth dough. you may not need all of it. knead 5 minutes, cover and rest at least 2 hours. pinch off marble-sized pieces. roll each into a tiny ball, press it flat on the back of a greased fork, then roll it away from you with your thumb so it curls into a shell. spread the shaped kalkals on a tray in a single layer and leave them to dry, uncovered, for 30 minutes. heat the oil in a kadhai to a steady medium — a scrap of dough should rise slowly and sizzle, not brown in seconds. fry in batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until pale gold and hard. drain on paper and cool completely. boil the 250g sugar with the water to a thick syrup: it is ready when a drop cooled on a plate forms a soft ball between your fingers. take the syrup off the heat, tip in the cooled kalkals and stir constantly as the syrup crystallises into a white frosting, 2 to 3 minutes. spread them out on a tray to dry and harden for an hour before storing.

entries.title: Mulligatawny Soup
entries.snippet: pepper water turned into a meal, thick with toor dal, shredded chicken and a spoon of rice
entries.text: mulligatawny soup anglo-indian pepper water turned into a meal, thick with toor dal, shredded chicken and a spoon of rice gluten-free nut-free healthier chicken toor dal (pigeon pea) rice (short/medium grain) onion carrot garlic ginger curry leaves black pepper coriander powder turmeric powder cumin seeds coconut milk lemon / lime butter coriander leaves (cilantro) water salt simmer the chicken thighs in the water with half the crushed pepper and a good pinch of salt for 25 minutes, skimming the grey foam off the top. lift out the chicken, let it cool enough to handle, then pull the meat off in shreds and set aside. keep the stock. add the drained toor dal to the stock and simmer 25 to 30 minutes until it has completely lost its shape. meanwhile melt the butter in a second pan and crackle the cumin seeds and curry leaves, about 20 seconds. add the onion and carrot and cook until the onion is soft and just turning gold, 8 minutes. stir in the garlic, ginger, coriander powder, turmeric and the remaining black pepper and fry 2 minutes. tip the fried mixture into the dal pot and simmer everything together 10 minutes. blend about half the soup smooth and return it to the pan; leave the rest with texture. return the shredded chicken, stir in the coconut milk and warm through for 5 minutes without letting it boil. check the salt. put a spoon of hot rice in each bowl, ladle the soup over, scatter coriander leaves and serve with lemon wedges.

entries.title: Mutton Cutlets
entries.snippet: flat spiced mince patties crumbed and shallow-fried until the coating shatters
entries.text: mutton cutlets anglo-indian flat spiced mince patties crumbed and shallow-fried until the coating shatters dairy-free nut-free mutton / lamb potato onion ginger garlic green chilli black pepper garam masala turmeric powder coriander leaves (cilantro) vinegar eggs sliced bread plain flour (maida) neutral oil lemon / lime salt cook the mince in a dry pan over medium heat with the onion, ginger, garlic and green chilli until the meat has lost its pink and the liquid has gone, 12 to 15 minutes. stir in the black pepper, garam masala, turmeric and 1 tsp salt and fry 2 more minutes. take off the heat and cool completely. work in the mashed potato, coriander leaves and vinegar. the mix should hold a shape when pressed. divide into 12 and shape each into a flat oval about 1cm thick. set up three plates: maida, beaten egg, breadcrumbs. dust each cutlet in flour, dip in egg, then press firmly into the crumbs. chill the crumbed cutlets 20 minutes. heat the oil on a tawa or wide frying pan over medium heat until a crumb dropped in sizzles steadily. fry in batches, 3 minutes a side, until deep golden brown and crisp. drain on paper and serve hot with lemon wedges and a sweet-sour chutney.

entries.title: Pepper Water
entries.snippet: the thin black-peppery tamarind broth mulligatawny was built on, drunk over plain rice
entries.text: pepper water anglo-indian the thin black-peppery tamarind broth mulligatawny was built on, drunk over plain rice vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free nut-free black pepper cumin seeds garlic tamarind toor dal (pigeon pea) tomato dried red chillies turmeric powder asafoetida (hing) mustard seeds curry leaves coconut oil coriander leaves (cilantro) water salt pound the black pepper, cumin seeds and 4 of the garlic cloves to a coarse, gritty paste. bring the strained tamarind water, the remaining water, the chopped tomato, turmeric and salt to a boil in a wide pan. boil hard for 5 minutes until the raw, puckering smell of the tamarind has gone. stir in the pounded pepper-cumin-garlic paste and simmer 8 minutes. if using, whisk the mashed toor dal with a ladle of the hot broth and stir it back in. simmer 3 minutes more. in a small pan heat the coconut oil, crackle the mustard seeds, then add the dried red chillies, the remaining bruised garlic and the curry leaves. stir in the asafoetida off the heat for 5 seconds and pour the whole tempering into the pepper water. cover at once and let it stand 2 minutes so the aromatics steep, then scatter the coriander leaves. serve very hot, either in cups on its own or poured over plain rice with a spoon of ghee.

entries.title: Railway Mutton Curry
entries.snippet: the mild dining-car mutton curry, loosened with coconut milk and sharpened with tamarind
entries.text: railway mutton curry anglo-indian the mild dining-car mutton curry, loosened with coconut milk and sharpened with tamarind gluten-free nut-free healthier mutton / lamb potato onion ginger garlic tomato coriander powder red chilli powder turmeric powder cumin powder (jeera) black pepper bay leaf cinnamon cloves tamarind coconut milk ghee curry leaves water salt heat the ghee in a pressure cooker and drop in the bay leaf, cinnamon and cloves. they should fizz and smell sweet within 30 seconds. add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and cook over medium heat until deep gold and collapsed, 12 to 14 minutes. stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes, until the raw edge is gone. add the coriander, chilli, turmeric and cumin powders with 3 tbsp water and fry 2 minutes. add the tomato and cook until it breaks down and ghee glosses the edge of the pan, 6 to 8 minutes. turn the heat high, add the mutton and brown it in the masala for 8 minutes, stirring so every piece is coated and the surface has sealed. pour in the water, salt to taste, close the cooker and cook 20 minutes at full pressure. let the pressure fall on its own. open, add the potato halves and simmer uncovered 12 to 15 minutes until a knife slides through them without resistance. stir in the strained tamarind water, the coconut milk and the crushed black pepper. simmer gently 6 to 8 minutes. fry the curry leaves in a teaspoon of ghee until they crackle and pour them over the curry. rest 10 minutes before serving with bread or yellow rice.

entries.title: Yellow Coconut Rice
entries.snippet: turmeric-gold rice steamed in coconut milk with whole spice, the standing partner to ball curry
entries.text: yellow coconut rice anglo-indian turmeric-gold rice steamed in coconut milk with whole spice, the standing partner to ball curry vegetarian gluten-free nut-free basmati rice coconut milk water turmeric powder onion cloves cinnamon bay leaf black pepper ghee sugar raisins (kishmish) salt heat the ghee in a heavy pan and fry the cloves, cinnamon, bay leaf and peppercorns for 30 seconds until fragrant. add the sliced onion and cook until pale gold and soft, 7 to 8 minutes. lift out a spoonful to scatter over later. stir in the turmeric and fry 20 seconds, then add the raisins if using. tip in the drained rice and turn it in the fat for 2 minutes, until every grain is coated and glossy. pour in the coconut milk and water, add the salt and sugar, and bring to a boil. as soon as it boils, drop the heat to the lowest setting, cover tightly and cook 12 minutes without lifting the lid. take the pan off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes more. fork the grains apart gently from the edge inwards, scatter the reserved onion over and serve.

entries.title: Aloo ki Tehri
entries.snippet: the one-pot turmeric rice and potato dinner every Lucknow household falls back on
entries.text: aloo ki tehri awadhi/lucknowi the one-pot turmeric rice and potato dinner every lucknow household falls back on vegetarian gluten-free nut-free healthier basmati rice potato peas onion ghee cumin seeds bay leaf cloves green cardamom cinnamon turmeric powder coriander powder green chilli ginger garam masala coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water heat the ghee in a heavy pot and crackle the cumin, bay leaf, cloves, cardamom and cinnamon for 30 seconds. add the onion and fry 8 minutes over medium heat, until evenly golden brown. add the ginger and green chillies, fry 1 minute, then the potato chunks. fry 5 minutes until their edges pick up colour. stir in the turmeric, coriander powder and salt with 2 tbsp water and cook 1 minute. add the drained rice and peas and turn everything over gently for 2 minutes, until every grain is coated and glossy. pour in the hot water, bring to a rolling boil, then taste for salt and let it boil uncovered 4 minutes until the water level drops to the rice. cover tightly, drop the heat to the lowest setting and cook 12 minutes without lifting the lid. take off the heat, sprinkle over the garam masala, and rest covered 10 minutes before opening. fluff with a fork, fold in the coriander leaves and serve with plain yogurt and a raw onion salad.

entries.title: Arhar ki Dal
entries.snippet: the plain everyday toor dal of Lucknow homes, finished with a loud ghee, cumin and hing tadka
entries.text: arhar ki dal awadhi/lucknowi the plain everyday toor dal of lucknow homes, finished with a loud ghee, cumin and hing tadka vegetarian gluten-free nut-free healthier toor dal (pigeon pea) turmeric powder tomato ghee cumin seeds asafoetida (hing) dried red chillies garlic ginger green chilli lemon / lime coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water put the dal, water, turmeric, tomato and half the salt in a pressure cooker. cook on high for 4 whistles, then let the pressure drop by itself, about 10 minutes. open up and whisk the dal briskly for 20 seconds. it should be loose and pourable, like thin cream — add hot water if it has tightened. add the slit green chillies and simmer uncovered 5 minutes so the dal takes on their scent. heat the ghee in a small pan until it shimmers. add the cumin and let it crackle and darken by a shade, about 15 seconds. drop in the hing, then the broken red chillies, then the sliced garlic and ginger. fry 30-40 seconds, until the garlic is pale gold. pour the tadka straight into the dal and clap the lid on for 2 minutes to trap the aroma. stir in the lemon juice and the rest of the salt off the heat, taste, and scatter the coriander leaves.

entries.title: Awadhi Kheer
entries.snippet: slow-reduced rice pudding scented with saffron, cardamom and a drop of kewra
entries.text: awadhi kheer awadhi/lucknowi slow-reduced rice pudding scented with saffron, cardamom and a drop of kewra vegetarian gluten-free no-onion-garlic milk basmati rice sugar ghee green cardamom saffron almonds pistachios raisins (kishmish) kewra water rub the pan with ghee, pour in the milk and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring. add the drained, crushed rice and lower the heat so the milk simmers gently. cook uncovered 45–50 minutes, stirring and scraping the base every 4–5 minutes, until the rice is soft and the milk has reduced by nearly half. push the cream that forms on the sides back into the pan as you go. add the sugar and stir 8 minutes until it dissolves and the kheer thickens again. stir in the saffron milk and cook 4 minutes until the colour is even. add the cardamom powder, almonds, pistachios and raisins and cook 2 minutes. take off the heat, stir in the kewra water, and let it stand 15 minutes. serve warm, or chill 2 hours and serve cold with extra slivered pistachios.

entries.title: Awadhi Murgh Masala
entries.snippet: everyday bone-in chicken curry, browned onion and yogurt with ground cashew, gentle on chilli
entries.text: awadhi murgh masala awadhi/lucknowi everyday bone-in chicken curry, browned onion and yogurt with ground cashew, gentle on chilli gluten-free healthier chicken yogurt / dahi onion cashews ghee ginger garlic tomato coriander powder cumin powder (jeera) kashmiri chilli powder turmeric powder garam masala green cardamom cloves cinnamon bay leaf kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) coriander leaves (cilantro) water salt heat the ghee, add the bay leaf, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and let them swell for 30 seconds. add the sliced onion and cook over medium heat, stirring, until deep golden brown, 12–14 minutes. stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 2 minutes until the raw smell goes. add the coriander powder, cumin powder, kashmiri chilli and 2 tbsp water and bhuno 2 minutes. add the chopped tomato, if using, and cook until it breaks down completely, 4 minutes. lower the flame, add the marinated chicken with all its yogurt and stir constantly for 8 minutes until the fat separates and the pieces are coated. blend the soaked cashews with 4 tbsp water to a smooth paste and stir it in with the salt. pour in 300ml warm water, cover and simmer 18–20 minutes until the chicken is tender and the gravy has thickened. uncover, add the garam masala and crushed kasuri methi and reduce 3 minutes. rest covered 5 minutes, scatter with coriander leaves and serve with paratha or rice.

entries.title: Awadhi Paneer Korma
entries.snippet: paneer in an ivory cashew and yogurt gravy, mild and heavily perfumed
entries.text: awadhi paneer korma awadhi/lucknowi paneer in an ivory cashew and yogurt gravy, mild and heavily perfumed vegetarian gluten-free healthier paneer yogurt / dahi onion cashews melon seeds (magaz) ghee cream ginger garlic green chilli coriander powder fennel powder green cardamom mace (javitri) white pepper saffron kewra water water salt fry the sliced onion in 2 tbsp ghee over medium heat until pale gold and soft, 8 minutes. do not let it brown. cool the onion and grind it with the soaked cashews, melon seeds and 4 tbsp water to a completely smooth paste. heat the remaining 2 tbsp ghee, add the ginger and garlic pastes and fry 90 seconds until the raw edge is gone. add the onion-cashew paste and cook on low for 6 minutes, stirring often, until it thickens and no longer smells raw. take the pan off the heat and whisk in the yogurt in three additions, then return to the lowest flame for 5 minutes until the ghee shows at the edges. stir in the coriander powder, fennel powder, mace, white pepper, green chillies and salt and cook 2 minutes. add 250ml warm water and simmer uncovered 6 minutes until the gravy coats a spoon. drain the paneer, slip it in and simmer 4 minutes only. finish with cream, cardamom powder, saffron milk and a few drops of kewra water. rest covered 5 minutes before serving.

entries.title: Bhindi do Pyaza
entries.snippet: dry-fried okra with twice its weight in onion, sharp with amchur and mustard oil
entries.text: bhindi do pyaza awadhi/lucknowi dry-fried okra with twice its weight in onion, sharp with amchur and mustard oil vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free nut-free okra / bhindi onion mustard oil cumin seeds turmeric powder coriander powder red chilli powder fennel powder amchur (dry mango powder) garam masala green chilli salt heat the mustard oil in a kadhai until it smokes faintly, then lower the heat and let it settle for 30 seconds. add the cumin seeds and let them crackle, 15 seconds, then tip in the okra with 1/2 tsp salt. fry the okra on medium-high heat, stirring only every couple of minutes, for 8-10 minutes, until the edges brown and the pods stop looking sticky. lift the okra out onto a plate. add the sliced onion to the same pan and cook 4 minutes until it softens and turns gold at the edges. add the onion petals and green chillies and fry 3 minutes on high — they should stay crunchy and separate, not collapse. lower the heat, add the turmeric, coriander, chilli and fennel powders with a splash of water and fry 1 minute to bloom the spices. return the okra, add the remaining salt and toss gently for 3 minutes until everything is coated. sprinkle over the amchur and garam masala, toss once and take off the heat immediately.

entries.title: Boti Kebab
entries.snippet: yogurt-marinated mutton cubes, charred outside and juicy through
entries.text: boti kebab awadhi/lucknowi yogurt-marinated mutton cubes, charred outside and juicy through gluten-free nut-free healthier mutton / lamb yogurt / dahi raw green papaya ginger garlic kashmiri chilli powder coriander powder garam masala black pepper mustard oil besan (gram flour) ghee lemon / lime chaat masala salt pat the mutton cubes completely dry and prick each one two or three times with a fork. rub in the papaya paste, ginger, garlic and salt and leave 20 minutes. whisk the hung yogurt with the roasted besan, kashmiri chilli, coriander powder, garam masala, black pepper and the cooled mustard oil until smooth. fold the meat through the marinade, cover and refrigerate overnight. thread onto skewers with a finger gap between cubes so the heat gets all the way round. grill over medium-hot charcoal or under an oven grill at 240c for 12–15 minutes, turning every 3 minutes. baste with ghee in the last 4 minutes and let the edges blacken in patches. rest 3 minutes off the heat, then dust with chaat masala and squeeze over lemon.

entries.title: Dahi ke Kebab
entries.snippet: crisp-shelled hung yogurt kebabs that dissolve into cream the moment you bite
entries.text: dahi ke kebab awadhi/lucknowi crisp-shelled hung yogurt kebabs that dissolve into cream the moment you bite vegetarian nut-free healthier yogurt / dahi paneer besan (gram flour) sliced bread onion green chilli ginger green cardamom white pepper chaat masala coriander leaves (cilantro) ghee salt tip the hung yogurt into a bowl and mash in the grated paneer until smooth and even. squeeze the chopped onion in your fist over the sink to wring out its water, then fold it in with the green chilli, ginger, cardamom, white pepper, coriander leaves and salt. work in the roasted besan a tablespoon at a time until the mixture just holds a shape when pressed. it should feel soft, almost too soft. rest the mix 15 minutes, then shape into 10 flat discs about 5cm across and 1.5cm thick with lightly oiled palms. press each disc into the breadcrumbs on both sides and on the rim, then chill 20 minutes on a lined tray. heat 2 tbsp ghee on a tawa over medium-low heat. lay in half the kebabs, leaving space between them. fry undisturbed 3-4 minutes, until the underside is set and deep gold, then turn once with a thin spatula and give the second side 3 minutes. drain briefly on paper, repeat with the rest, dust with chaat masala and serve hot with mint chutney.

entries.title: Dum Aloo Lucknowi
entries.snippet: fried baby potatoes finished in a yogurt gravy with fennel and dry ginger, no onion or garlic
entries.text: dum aloo lucknowi awadhi/lucknowi fried baby potatoes finished in a yogurt gravy with fennel and dry ginger, no onion or garlic vegetarian gluten-free no-onion-garlic nut-free potato yogurt / dahi ghee neutral oil asafoetida (hing) fennel powder dry ginger powder (saunth) coriander powder kashmiri chilli powder turmeric powder cumin seeds green cardamom cloves cinnamon bay leaf garam masala kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves) water salt prick the boiled, peeled potatoes deeply all over and pat them dry. deep fry them in hot oil until golden and lightly blistered, 4–5 minutes. drain and set aside. whisk the yogurt with the coriander powder, kashmiri chilli, turmeric, fennel powder and dry ginger powder to a smooth, lump-free mix. heat the ghee in a kadhai, add the bay leaf, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and cumin seeds and let them crackle 30 seconds. add the asafoetida, count to five, then immediately pour in the spiced yogurt. cook on the lowest flame, stirring without stopping, for 7–8 minutes until the mixture thickens and the ghee separates. add the fried potatoes and salt and turn them through the masala for 3 minutes. pour in 250ml warm water, bring to a simmer, then cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes. uncover, stir in the garam masala and crushed kasuri methi and reduce 3 minutes until the gravy clings to the potatoes. rest covered 5 minutes before serving with sheermal or plain rice.

entries.title: Galouti Kebab
entries.snippet: Minced mutton kebabs so soft they collapse on the tongue, from the Nawab's kitchen
entries.text: galouti kebab awadhi/lucknowi minced mutton kebabs so soft they collapse on the tongue, from the nawab's kitchen gluten-free healthier mutton / lamb raw green papaya ghee onion cashews garam masala mace (javitri) nutmeg green cardamom ginger garlic saffron besan (gram flour) salt blend the mince to a smooth paste with the papaya, ginger and garlic. rest 45 minutes, refrigerated. fry the sliced onion in ghee until deep brown, drain, cool and crush to a powder. this birista carries most of the sweetness. work the birista, ground cashew, garam masala, mace, nutmeg, cardamom, saffron milk and salt into the mince. it should be soft but hold a shape; add the roasted besan only if it will not. chill the mix 30 minutes, then shape into flat discs about 6cm across and 1cm thick. fry on a tawa in ghee over low-medium heat, 3-4 minutes a side. turn once and gently — they are fragile. serve immediately with ulte tawe ka paratha or plain sheermal.

entries.title: Kakori Kebab
entries.snippet: silky skewered mutton mince, perfumed with mace and khoya, that barely holds its shape
entries.text: kakori kebab awadhi/lucknowi silky skewered mutton mince, perfumed with mace and khoya, that barely holds its shape gluten-free mutton / lamb raw green papaya onion ghee khoya / mawa cashews almonds poppy seeds (khus khus) ginger garlic mace (javitri) nutmeg green cardamom white pepper garam masala saffron kewra water salt fry the sliced onion in 3 tbsp ghee over medium heat until evenly deep brown, 10–12 minutes. drain, cool until crisp, then crush to a powder. blend the mince with the papaya paste, ginger and garlic to a smooth, almost creamy paste. work in the birista powder, ground cashew, almond, poppy seed, khoya, mace, nutmeg, cardamom, white pepper, garam masala, saffron milk, kewra and salt. cover and refrigerate 2 hours, then chill in the freezer 15 minutes just before shaping. wet your palm and press the mince along a flat skewer in a sausage about 15cm long and 2cm thick, tapering the ends. grill over medium charcoal or in an oven at 220c, turning every 3 minutes and basting with ghee, for 12–15 minutes total. finish 1 minute directly over high heat to colour the outside. slide off the skewer, rest 2 minutes, and serve with sheermal and onion rings.

entries.title: Kali Mirch ka Murgh
entries.snippet: pale peppery chicken in a white onion-and-cashew gravy with no chilli at all
entries.text: kali mirch ka murgh awadhi/lucknowi pale peppery chicken in a white onion-and-cashew gravy with no chilli at all gluten-free healthier chicken black pepper white pepper onion cashews yogurt / dahi ginger garlic ghee green cardamom cloves bay leaf cream coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water heat the ghee on medium and drop in the bay leaf, cloves and cardamom. give them 30 seconds, until they puff and perfume the fat. add the boiled onion paste and cook 6-7 minutes, stirring often, until it loses its raw smell but stays ivory. stir in the cashew paste and cook 3 minutes more, until the mixture thickens and pulls away from the base. add the marinated chicken with all its yogurt and fry on medium heat for 6 minutes, until the pieces turn opaque and firm. add the salt, pour in the hot water, cover and simmer 18-20 minutes, until the chicken is tender and the gravy coats a spoon. uncover and stir in the remaining black pepper and the white pepper. simmer 3 minutes so the heat blooms in the gravy. swirl in the cream, take off the heat and rest 5 minutes covered. scatter the coriander leaves and serve with roomali roti or plain steamed rice.

entries.title: Kathal ki Sabzi
entries.snippet: raw jackfruit browned in mustard oil and simmered in a dark bhuna masala, meaty enough to fool anyone
entries.text: kathal ki sabzi awadhi/lucknowi raw jackfruit browned in mustard oil and simmered in a dark bhuna masala, meaty enough to fool anyone vegetarian vegan gluten-free dairy-free nut-free healthier raw jackfruit (kathal) mustard oil onion tomato ginger garlic cumin seeds bay leaf black cardamom turmeric powder coriander powder red chilli powder fennel powder garam masala coriander leaves (cilantro) salt water heat 4 tbsp mustard oil in a kadhai and fry the jackfruit in two batches over medium heat, 6-7 minutes a batch, turning until the pieces are gold on all faces. drain and set aside. add the remaining 2 tbsp oil, then the cumin, bay leaf and black cardamom. let them crackle 30 seconds. add the sliced onion and fry 10-12 minutes over medium heat until deep brown at the edges. stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and cook 2 minutes, until the sharp smell lifts. add the turmeric, coriander, chilli and fennel powders with 2 tbsp water and fry 1 minute. pour in the tomato puree and salt. bhuno on medium heat 8-10 minutes, until the masala darkens and oil beads out at the sides. return the jackfruit, turn it through the masala for 2 minutes, then add the hot water. cover and simmer on low 15-18 minutes, until a knife slides into a piece with no resistance and the gravy clings. sprinkle the garam masala, cover off the heat for 5 minutes, then finish with the coriander leaves.

entries.title: Lucknowi Dum Biryani
entries.snippet: Pakki biryani: meat and rice cooked separately, then sealed and finished on dum
